row.title: DSA patterns
row.summaryMd: Pattern guides and full articles for the DSA roadmap. Each pattern has a short guide and, where written, an article.

blocks.body: Every design sits on the network path: client → DNS → CDN/edge → load balancer → service → data store. Know what each hop costs and what it can do for you (caching, TLS termination, routing), because latency and failure modes come from here.
A 1 by 1 pixel test image.

TCP gives an ordered, reliable byte stream with flow and congestion control, at the cost of a handshake and head-of-line blocking. UDP sends independent datagrams with no delivery guarantee; use it when late data is useless (voice, video, games) or when you build reliability yourself (QUIC).

HTTP/1.1 allows one in-flight request per connection, so browsers open ~6 connections. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection with header compression, but a lost TCP packet stalls every stream. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP), so streams are independent and connection setup is faster.

TLS 1.3 needs one round trip: the client sends supported ciphers and a key share, the server replies with its key share and certificate, and both derive symmetric keys (ECDHE). Asymmetric crypto is only used to agree on keys; bulk data uses fast symmetric encryption (AES-GCM). Resumption allows 0-RTT.

The resolver checks its cache, then asks a root server, the TLD server (.com) and the domain's authoritative server, caching each answer for its TTL. Low TTLs allow fast failover but cost more lookups; DNS can return different IPs per region (GeoDNS) to route users nearby.

A CDN caches content at edge locations close to users, cutting latency and origin load. Static assets are the obvious case; it can also cache API responses with short TTLs, terminate TLS, absorb DDoS traffic and run edge logic. Invalidate by versioned URLs rather than purges where possible.

L4 balancers route by IP and port without reading the payload: very fast, protocol-agnostic. L7 balancers parse HTTP, so they can route by path or header, terminate TLS, retry, and do sticky sessions. Common algorithms: round robin, least connections, consistent hashing (for cache affinity).

A forward proxy acts for clients (corporate egress, anonymity). A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and acts for them: TLS termination, compression, caching, rate limiting, routing to backends. Nginx, Envoy and HAProxy are typical; an API gateway is a reverse proxy with auth and API-level policies.
Request path: DNS → CDN/edge → L4/L7 load balancer → service → cache/DB.
TCP handshake 1 RTT + TLS 1.3 1 RTT before the first byte; reuse connections.
HTTP/2 multiplexes but suffers TCP head-of-line blocking; HTTP/3 (QUIC over UDP) fixes it.
L4 = fast, protocol-agnostic; L7 = route by path/header, TLS termination, retries.

sections.title: Worked example: what a cold request costs

blocks.body:
User in Mumbai, origin in us-east (≈200 ms RTT). Cold: DNS lookup (cache miss, ~50-100 ms), TCP handshake (1 RTT = 200 ms), TLS 1.3 (1 RTT = 200 ms), request + response (1 RTT = 200 ms) → ~650 ms before any server time.

With a CDN PoP in Mumbai (≈10 ms RTT) terminating TLS and keeping warm connections to the origin: handshakes cost ~20 ms, and cached content returns in ~30 ms total. That's why designs put TLS termination and caching at the edge, and why connection reuse (keep-alive, HTTP/2) matters more than raw bandwidth.

TCP turns an unreliable packet network into a reliable, ordered byte stream. The handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) agrees on starting sequence numbers. Every byte has a sequence number; the receiver acknowledges what it has received in order (cumulative ACKs), and the sender retransmits anything not acknowledged in time or after three duplicate ACKs (fast retransmit). Flow control uses the receiver's advertised window so a fast sender can't overflow a slow receiver; congestion control (slow start, then additive increase / multiplicative decrease, or BBR) keeps the sender from overwhelming the network.

The costs: one round trip before any data, head-of-line blocking (a lost segment holds back everything after it, even data for unrelated requests), and per-connection state in the kernel. That's why connection reuse matters and why HTTP/3 moved to QUIC.

UDP sends independent datagrams with an 8-byte header: no handshake, no ordering, no retransmission, no congestion control. The application decides what to do with loss. It fits DNS (one small question, one small answer, retry on timeout), real-time media (a late voice packet is worthless), games (send the latest state, ignore old), and protocols that build their own reliability (QUIC, many VPNs). In a design, say UDP only when late data is useless or you're consciously re-implementing reliability.

sections.title: HTTP versions and what they change for a system

blocks.body:
HTTP/1.1 keeps connections alive but serves one request at a time per connection (pipelining exists but is effectively unused), so browsers open about 6 connections per host and developers used tricks like domain sharding and sprite sheets. Each response is text headers plus a body; headers repeat on every request.

HTTP/2 is binary and multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection, with HPACK header compression and stream priorities. One connection per host is enough, which reduces handshakes and helps TLS and congestion windows warm up. Its weakness is TCP: a single lost packet stalls every stream on the connection, which hurts on lossy mobile networks. gRPC is built on HTTP/2 and uses its streaming.

HTTP/3 runs HTTP over QUIC on UDP. Streams are independent at the transport level, so loss on one doesn't block the others; the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes are combined (1 RTT, 0-RTT on resumption); and connections survive IP changes (Wi-Fi to cellular) because they're identified by connection IDs. The cost is more CPU in user space and some networks that block or throttle UDP, so clients fall back to HTTP/2.

For a design answer: terminate HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 at the edge (CDN or load balancer) for clients, and use HTTP/2 or gRPC with long-lived pooled connections between internal services.

sections.title: CDNs, proxies and gateways: what sits where

blocks.body:
A CDN is a network of edge servers (PoPs) near users. With a pull CDN, the edge fetches from your origin on the first miss and caches according to Cache-Control; with a push CDN you upload content ahead of time. Static assets get long TTLs with versioned file names; HTML and API responses get short TTLs or are passed through. CDNs also terminate TLS close to the user, absorb DDoS traffic, apply WAF rules, and can run small functions at the edge (redirects, A/B bucketing, auth token checks). Origin shielding (one regional cache in front of the origin) stops every PoP from hitting the origin on a miss.

A reverse proxy (Nginx, Envoy, HAProxy) sits in front of your servers: TLS termination, compression, routing by host/path, request buffering (protects app servers from slow clients), caching, rate limiting, retries and health-checked load balancing. A forward proxy sits in front of clients (corporate egress, outbound allow-lists, outgoing request logging).

An API gateway is a reverse proxy specialized for APIs: authentication (validate JWT or API keys), per-client quotas, request validation, routing to services, protocol translation (REST to gRPC), and API analytics. A service mesh handles the same concerns between internal services with sidecar proxies.

Typical layering: DNS → CDN/WAF → regional L4 load balancer → L7 gateway → services → caches and databases. Draw it once early in a design and refer back to it.

sections.title: Load balancer algorithms and when each fits

blocks.body:
Round robin: equal servers, similar requests. Weighted round robin: mixed instance sizes. Least connections / least outstanding requests: long or uneven requests (uploads, streaming). Power of two choices: pick two random servers, send to the less loaded; nearly as good as least-connections with no global state. Consistent hashing on a key: cache affinity (same user → same cache node) at the cost of uneven load for hot keys.

Health checks remove dead backends; connection draining lets in-flight requests finish during deploys. The balancer itself is made redundant with an active-passive pair sharing a virtual IP, or several balancers behind DNS / anycast.

points: Long polling vs SSE vs WebSockets

blocks.body: The API is the contract between clients and your system. Interviewers look for clear resources, safe retries (idempotency), sensible pagination and the right real-time mechanism for the use case.

REST: resources and HTTP verbs, cacheable, universal; the default for public APIs. gRPC: Protobuf over HTTP/2, typed contracts, streaming, fast; good between internal services. GraphQL: the client asks for exactly the fields it needs in one round trip; good for varied frontends, but harder to cache and to protect from expensive queries.

The client sends a unique Idempotency-Key with a non-idempotent request (e.g. POST /payments). The server stores key → result; a retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of charging twice. Store keys with a TTL (e.g. 24 h) and make the 'check and insert' atomic.

Offset pagination (LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000) is simple but slow for deep pages and skips or repeats rows when data changes. Cursor/keyset pagination (WHERE id < last_seen ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20) uses an index, is stable under inserts, and scales; return an opaque cursor to the client.

Version so old clients keep working: in the URL (/v1/…), a header, or by only making backward-compatible changes (add optional fields, never remove or rename). Deprecate with a timeline and usage metrics.

Protect the API from abuse and noisy clients by limiting requests per key, user or IP. Return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After. Usually enforced at the gateway with a token bucket backed by Redis.

Webhooks push events to a URL the customer registers, instead of the customer polling. Sign payloads (HMAC) so receivers can verify them, retry with backoff, and expect receivers to dedupe because delivery is at-least-once.

sections.title: Long polling vs SSE vs WebSockets

blocks.body: Long polling: the client's request is held open until there's data, then it re-requests; works everywhere. Server-Sent Events: one long-lived HTTP response streaming server→client events; simple, auto-reconnects. WebSockets: full-duplex over one connection; needed for chat or games, but stateful connections complicate load balancing.
Public: REST; internal service-to-service: gRPC; many client shapes: GraphQL.
POST + Idempotency-Key header, server stores key → response for ~24 h.
Cursor pagination for feeds: WHERE (created_at, id) < cursor ORDER BY … LIMIT n.
Chat/games → WebSockets; one-way live updates → SSE; fallback → long polling.

Start from the use cases and turn nouns into resources: /users/{id}, /orders/{id}, /orders/{id}/items. Use HTTP methods for intent: GET reads (safe, cacheable), POST creates or triggers actions, PUT replaces, PATCH updates partially, DELETE removes. Return the created resource's id and location on POST (201 Created + Location header).

Good status codes help clients: 400 for invalid input (with field-level errors), 401 for missing/invalid credentials, 403 for authenticated but not allowed, 404 for missing resources (or to hide existence), 409 for conflicts (version mismatch, duplicate), 422 for semantically invalid requests, 429 for rate limits, 503 for temporary unavailability with Retry-After.

Use a consistent error body ({code, message, details, requestId}) so clients and support can correlate with logs. Accept and return timestamps in ISO-8601 UTC, money as integer minor units with a currency code, and ids as opaque strings so you can change their format later.

For actions that aren't CRUD (cancel an order, retry a payment), either model them as sub-resources (POST /orders/{id}/cancellation) or as explicit action endpoints; both are fine if consistent. For long-running work, return 202 Accepted with a job/operation resource the client can poll or be notified about.

sections.title: gRPC and GraphQL in more depth

blocks.body:
gRPC defines services and messages in Protobuf. Code is generated for clients and servers, so contracts are typed and changes are checked at compile time. Messages are compact binary, and HTTP/2 enables four call types: unary, server streaming, client streaming and bidirectional streaming. Deadlines propagate across calls, and status codes are standardized. Protobuf evolves safely when you only add fields with new numbers and never reuse removed numbers. Downsides: browsers can't call gRPC directly (gRPC-Web or a gateway translates), payloads aren't human-readable, and HTTP caching doesn't apply.

GraphQL exposes a typed schema; clients send a query naming exactly the fields they need, possibly across related objects, in one round trip. That's great for mobile and for many different frontends. Costs: every query is a POST to one endpoint, so CDN caching needs persisted queries; resolvers can trigger N+1 database calls unless batched with a DataLoader; and arbitrary queries can be expensive, so you need depth/complexity limits and timeouts. Authorization must be enforced per field or per resolver.

A common real-world split: GraphQL or REST at the edge for clients (often a backend-for-frontend per app), gRPC between internal services, and events (Kafka) for asynchronous integration.

Client generates a UUID per logical operation and retries with the same key. Server: INSERT INTO idempotency(key, status='in_progress') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. If the insert won, do the work and store the response; if it lost, return the stored response (or 409 if still in progress). Wrap 'do the work + store response' in one transaction when they share a database.

Scope keys per user/merchant so two customers can't collide, compare the request body hash so the same key with a different payload is rejected (422), and expire keys after a window.

Sorting by created_at alone breaks when two rows share a timestamp. Sort by (created_at DESC, id DESC) and encode both in the cursor. The query uses a composite index and costs the same on page 1 and page 10,000, while OFFSET 200000 scans and throws away 200k rows.

Return next_cursor = base64({created_at, id}) of the last row. You can't jump to page N; for UIs that need it, cap offsets (e.g. 10 pages) or precompute page boundaries.

code.text:
SELECT id, created_at, body FROM posts
WHERE user_id = $1 AND (created_at, id) < ($2, $3)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- index: (user_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)

sections.title: Webhooks and real-time delivery, done reliably

blocks.body:
Webhooks: the provider POSTs an event to a URL the customer configured. Make them dependable on both sides. Provider side: put events on a queue, deliver with a short timeout, retry with exponential backoff for hours or days, give up into a dead-letter list visible in a dashboard, and let customers replay events. Sign each payload with HMAC-SHA256 over the body and a timestamp; receivers verify the signature and reject old timestamps to stop replays. Send an event id so receivers can dedupe, because delivery is at-least-once and order isn't guaranteed (include a version or timestamp so receivers can ignore stale updates).

Receiver side: verify the signature, store the event, return 2xx quickly, then process asynchronously. Never do slow work before answering.

Real-time to browsers and apps: long polling works everywhere but costs a request per message batch. Server-Sent Events stream text events over one HTTP response and reconnect automatically with Last-Event-ID, which suits notifications, feeds and progress updates (server to client only). WebSockets give full-duplex messages for chat, collaboration and games. Because WebSocket connections are stateful and long-lived, you need a connection registry (which gateway holds which user), heartbeats, reconnect with resume from the last received message id, and load balancers configured for long connections. Mobile apps in the background rely on push notifications (APNs/FCM) instead.

A cache keeps hot data in fast storage (memory) to cut latency and load on the source. The hard parts aren't putting things in, but keeping them correct (invalidation) and surviving cache failures and stampedes.

Cache-aside: the app checks the cache, on a miss reads the DB and fills the cache; the most common pattern. Read-through: the cache itself loads from the DB on a miss. Write-through: writes go to cache and DB synchronously (fresh cache, slower writes). Write-behind: write to cache, flush to DB asynchronously (fast writes, risk of loss).

A TTL bounds staleness and frees memory automatically. Eviction kicks in when memory is full: LRU evicts the least recently used item (good default), LFU the least frequently used (better for stable popularity). Add jitter to TTLs so many keys don't expire at once.

When a hot key expires, thousands of requests miss at once and all hit the DB. Fixes: one request recomputes while others wait or get the stale value (lock or request coalescing), refresh early before expiry (probabilistic early expiration), or never expire hot keys and refresh them in the background.
A single key can overload one cache node (a viral post). Fixes: replicate the key with suffixes across nodes, add a small in-process cache in front, or use the CDN.

The safest approach is to delete the cache entry after writing the DB (not update it), with a TTL as a backstop. Races can still leave stale data briefly (a reader fills an old value after your delete); delayed double-delete or versioned keys reduce this. Change data capture can drive invalidation.

Redis: rich data structures (sorted sets, lists, hashes), persistence options, replication and clustering, pub/sub and Lua scripts; mostly single-threaded per shard. Memcached: a simple multi-threaded key-value cache with no persistence; good for plain large caches. Redis is the usual default.

CDNs cache responses at the edge using HTTP headers (Cache-Control: max-age, s-maxage, stale-while-revalidate). Version static asset URLs (app.3f2a.js) so they can be cached forever; give dynamic content short TTLs or don't cache it.
Cache-aside default: read cache → miss → DB → set with TTL; on write update DB then delete the key.
Stampede fixes: single-flight lock, early probabilistic refresh, serve stale while revalidating.
Hot key: replicate it across nodes or keep a tiny in-process cache.
Always set TTLs; they bound the damage of any invalidation bug.

Cache-aside (lazy loading): the application reads the cache, on a miss reads the database and fills the cache. Only requested data is cached and the cache can fail without breaking reads; the first request after a miss or expiry is slow, and the app owns invalidation. The default for most designs.

Read-through: the cache library or service loads from the database itself on a miss; same behaviour as cache-aside but the logic lives in the cache layer (e.g. a caching proxy, DAX for DynamoDB).

Write-through: writes go to the cache and synchronously to the database, so the cache is always fresh for written keys; writes are slower and you cache data that may never be read.

Write-behind (write-back): writes go to the cache and are flushed to the database asynchronously in batches. Very fast writes and absorbs spikes, but data is lost if the cache dies before flushing, and ordering/consistency gets harder. Use for counters, metrics, or with a durable log.

Refresh-ahead: proactively refresh popular entries before they expire, so users never see the miss penalty for hot keys.

Size the cache for the working set, not all data: 100M users × 1 KB profile = 100 GB total, but if 20% are active daily, ~20 GB keeps the hit rate high. Measure hit rate; below ~80% the cache may be adding latency without saving much.

LRU fits recency-driven access; LFU (Redis allkeys-lfu) protects popular items from being flushed by a one-off scan. Redis vs Memcached: Redis has data structures, persistence, replication and Lua; Memcached is a simple multithreaded key-value cache that scales vertically well. Most designs say Redis.

sections.title: Failure modes and how to handle them

blocks.body:
Cache stampede (thundering herd): a hot key expires and thousands of requests miss at once, all hitting the database. Fixes: single-flight (one request recomputes while others wait or get the stale value), probabilistic early expiration (each read has a small chance of refreshing before expiry), soft TTLs (serve stale while one background refresh runs), and jittered TTLs so many keys don't expire together.

Cache penetration: requests for keys that don't exist always miss and hit the database (often attacks). Cache negative results briefly or put a Bloom filter of valid keys in front.

Cache avalanche: the cache cluster restarts or a large fraction of keys expire together, and the database is overwhelmed. Fixes: replicas and persistence for the cache, warm-up before taking traffic, rate limiting and load shedding to the database, and staggered TTLs.

Hot keys: one key gets a huge share of traffic on one cache node. Replicate it (key#1..key#n across nodes), add a local in-process cache layer with a short TTL, or serve it from the CDN.

Inconsistency: write-then-invalidate races; mitigate with TTLs, versioning and CDC-driven invalidation.

sections.title: Why 'delete on write' beats 'update on write'

blocks.body:
Writer A sets price=10, writer B sets price=12. If each also updates the cache, the cache can end at 10 while the DB says 12 (B's cache write landed first). Deleting the key instead means the next reader loads the current DB value.

A race remains: a reader misses, reads the old value from the DB, a writer updates the DB and deletes the key, then the reader writes the old value into the cache. Mitigations: short TTLs, delayed double delete, or versioned values (only set if newer). For strict needs, invalidate from the DB's change stream (CDC) so the order follows commit order.

code.text:
def get_product(id):
    v = cache.get(f"product:{id}")
    if v is not None:
        return v
    with single_flight(f"product:{id}"):          # one loader per key
        v = db.query("SELECT ... WHERE id = %s", id)
        cache.set(f"product:{id}", v, ttl=300 + random(0, 60))   # jitter TTLs
    return v

def update_price(id, price):
    db.execute("UPDATE products SET price = %s WHERE id = %s", price, id)
    cache.delete(f"product:{id}")

blocks.body:
Client: browser HTTP cache, service worker, mobile app storage; controlled by Cache-Control and ETags. Edge: CDN caches static assets and cacheable API responses near users. Service: in-process memory caches (Caffeine, Guava) give nanosecond reads but each instance has its own copy (inconsistency across instances, memory per instance), so use short TTLs or invalidation messages. Distributed: Redis or Memcached shared by all instances: one network hop (~0.5 ms), one source of cached truth, scalable via sharding. Database: the buffer pool caches pages; materialized views cache query results.

Layering is normal: a hot product page might come from the CDN; on miss from the service's local cache; then Redis; then the database. Each layer needs a TTL and an invalidation story, and each extra layer makes 'why am I seeing old data?' harder to debug, so add layers only where the numbers justify them.

A celebrity's profile key is melting one Redis node. Fix it.
How do you stop a thundering herd when a hot key expires?
Caching without a plan for invalidation.
Treating the cache as a source of truth without persistence.

points: What you give up in a partition

blocks.body: CAP says that during a network partition, a distributed store must choose between consistency (refuse or delay requests) and availability (answer, possibly with stale data). PACELC adds that even without partitions there's a trade-off between latency and consistency.

sections.title: What you give up in a partition

blocks.body: Partitions happen (switches fail, links drop), so P isn't optional. When nodes can't talk, a CP system rejects writes or reads on the minority side to stay consistent (ZooKeeper, etcd, Spanner); an AP system keeps accepting them and reconciles later (Dynamo-style stores, Cassandra at low consistency levels).

PACELC: if Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. Synchronous replication to a quorum gives consistency but adds latency to every write even on a healthy network. DynamoDB and Cassandra are PA/EL by default; Spanner is PC/EC.
Partitions happen; during one choose C (refuse) or A (answer, maybe stale).
PACELC: else (no partition), trade Latency vs Consistency.
Spanner/etcd: PC/EC. Dynamo/Cassandra (default): PA/EL.

Two data centers replicate a shopping cart; the link between them drops. CP choice: the minority side rejects writes (errors for those users) so the cart never diverges. AP choice: both sides accept writes and merge later (Dynamo's cart unions items, so a deleted item can reappear).

CAP says nothing about the normal case, which is most of the time. PACELC adds it: even without partitions, synchronous replication to another region adds ~100 ms per write (consistency) while async replication is fast but can lose recent writes on failover (latency). Most real choices are the EL/EC ones.

CAP: in the presence of a network partition, a distributed system can't be both consistent (linearizable) and available (every request to a non-failing node gets a non-error response). So during a partition you choose: refuse or delay some requests (CP) or answer them possibly with stale or conflicting data (AP).

What it doesn't say: it's not 'pick two of three' in normal operation, since without a partition you can have both. Partitions aren't optional, since networks do fail, so 'CA' isn't a real choice for a distributed system. C means linearizability specifically, and A is a strong definition; many real systems are neither fully CP nor fully AP and make different choices per operation.

Use CAP in interviews to explain a specific behaviour: 'if the link between regions fails, this cart service keeps accepting writes in both regions (AP) and merges later, while the payment ledger rejects writes in the minority region (CP) because double spending is unacceptable.'

With N replicas, a write waits for W acks and a read queries R replicas. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps the latest write set, so a read can see the latest value (with versioning to pick it). N=3, W=2, R=2 is the common balance; W=1, R=1 is fast and eventually consistent; W=3 makes writes unavailable if any replica is down.

Quorums alone aren't linearizable (concurrent writes, sloppy quorums, failed writes partially applied); systems add read repair, hinted handoff and anti-entropy to converge.

PACELC extends CAP: if there's a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency. The else-branch is the one you live with every day.

PA/EL (Dynamo, Cassandra with low consistency levels): stay available during partitions, and favour low latency normally by not waiting for many replicas. PC/EC (Spanner, etcd, ZooKeeper, HBase): refuse writes without a majority during partitions, and pay coordination latency normally. PA/EC (some configurations of MongoDB historically): available in partitions, consistent reads from the primary normally. PC/EL is rare.

Practical consequence: a globally consistent database means writes wait for cross-region acknowledgement (tens to hundreds of milliseconds). If your product needs sub-50 ms writes worldwide, you either accept weaker consistency, partition data by region (each user's data is strongly consistent within its home region), or redesign the operation to be commutative.

sections.title: Making the choice in a design

blocks.body:
Go feature by feature. Ask: what's the cost of showing stale data, and what's the cost of rejecting a request? Like counts, view counts, feeds and recommendations: stale is fine, rejecting is bad (AP, eventual). Seat booking, inventory decrement, money movement, unique usernames: wrong data is very costly, so prefer CP for those operations, with a clear error and retry.

You can mix within one system: the order service accepts orders in each region (AP) but the payment authorization and inventory reservation run against a strongly consistent store, and if that's unreachable the order waits in 'pending'. Also mention detection and repair: if you choose AP, you need reconciliation jobs, idempotent merges and monitoring for divergence.
Is your design CP or AP during a partition, and what does the user see?
Why is 'CA' not a real option for a distributed system?
Treating CAP as 'pick 2 of 3' for the whole system; the choice can differ per operation (tunable consistency).

architecture.name: Shortener API
architecture.role: Accepts a long URL, takes the next id from a local block, scrambles it, encodes it in base62 and inserts the row with a unique constraint.
architecture.scale: About 39 writes a second on average (100 million a month). A few stateless servers are plenty; the id block means one allocator call per 1,000 writes.
architecture.failure: If one server dies, the others carry on and the unused part of its block (up to 999 ids) is wasted, which is nothing against 3.5 trillion codes.

architecture.name: Id block allocator
architecture.role: Hands each API server a block of 1,000 consecutive ids in one call, so no network call is needed per URL.
architecture.scale: One row or ZooKeeper counter that is called once per 1,000 writes across the fleet. Easily one small replicated node.
architecture.failure: If it is down, servers keep writing until their block runs out: about 250 seconds at 4 ids a second each. Redirects are not affected. A 10,000-id block stretches that to 40 minutes.

architecture.name: URL store
architecture.role: Holds code, long URL, owner, expiry and flags. Every access is by code, so it shards by hash of the code.
architecture.scale: 100 million rows a month at about 500 bytes is 6 billion rows and 3 TB over five years. Spread over a few shards with replicas.
architecture.failure: A down shard fails only its own codes, and a replica can be promoted. The unique constraint on the code is the final guard against duplicates.

architecture.name: Redis cache
architecture.role: Answers redirects from memory and falls back to the store on a miss. Each entry lives for the smaller of an hour and the time to expiry.
architecture.scale: The hottest 1 percent (1 million links) at about 120 bytes is roughly 120 MB. Expect a hit ratio above 90 percent, cutting 20,000 reads a second at peak to under 2,000.
architecture.failure: If a node dies, misses jump about 10 times and fall on the database. Use a replicated cluster, warm the replacement and coalesce concurrent misses for the same code.

architecture.name: Click pipeline (Kafka and aggregator)
architecture.role: The redirect service publishes a click event without waiting, and an aggregator counts clicks per link.
architecture.scale: Around 4,000 events a second on average, 20,000 at peak, each a few dozen bytes. Small for a Kafka topic.
architecture.failure: If Kafka is down, drop or buffer events locally. A few lost counts are acceptable; a slow redirect is not.

criteria.strong: Derives about 39 writes a second, 100 to 1 reads, a 20,000 a second peak and 3 TB over five years, then says the load is small and the hard parts are the code and the cache.
criteria.weak: Says billions of URLs with no arithmetic and sizes servers by guess.

criteria.strong: Compares hash-and-truncate, random, a global counter and block-allocated ids, quotes the birthday collision estimate, and picks block ids with a reversible scramble.
criteria.weak: Proposes a random or hashed code and never mentions collisions or what happens when one occurs.

criteria.strong: Puts a cache in front of a code-keyed store, sizes it (about 120 MB for the hot 1 percent), and uses 302 so clicks and expiry still work.
criteria.weak: Reads the database on every redirect, or uses 301 without noticing that analytics and takedowns stop working.

criteria.strong: Walks through cache loss, allocator outage (block lifetime in seconds), a hot shard and a viral link, and says reads take priority over writes.
criteria.weak: Says the system is replicated and stops; cannot say what happens when the id source or the cache is down.

criteria.strong: Covers custom aliases under the same unique constraint, expiry checked on read plus a sweeper, creation rate limits and a safe-browsing check.
criteria.weak: Treats the shortener as pure throughput and ignores phishing, expiry and alias races.

blocks.caption: Most redirects are answered from the cache without touching the database.

blocks.body: Options: (1) hash the URL (MD5 → first 7 chars) and handle collisions by retrying with a salt, which also dedupes identical URLs; (2) a counter/ID service handing out ranges to each app server, base62-encoded: no collisions, but codes are guessable (shuffle bits or add a random component if that matters); (3) pre-generate random codes into a key pool table and hand them out. Range-based counters are the simplest robust answer.

301 (permanent) lets browsers cache the redirect, cutting load but losing click analytics and the ability to change the target. 302 (temporary) sends every click through you. Most shorteners use 302 for analytics.
A viral link is a hot key: the cache absorbs it (plus CDN). Expired links: check expires_at on read and delete lazily, with a background cleanup job.

Start from the requirements, because they set every other choice. 100 million new URLs a month is 100,000,000 / (30 x 86,400) = about 39 writes a second on average. With a read-to-write ratio of 100 to 1, that is about 3,900 redirects a second on average, and a peak of perhaps 5 times the average, about 20,000 a second. Neither number is large: one well-tuned Redis node handles 100,000 operations a second, and a few application servers handle 20,000 redirects. The design is not about raw throughput. It is about three other things: a code that never collides, a cache that absorbs the hot links, and a read path that stays up when parts of the system are down.

Storage: a row holds the code (7 bytes), the long URL (average perhaps 100 bytes, with 2,000 as the practical limit), a user id, two timestamps and some flags. Budgeting 500 bytes per row, 100 million rows a month for five years is 6 billion rows and 3 TB. That fits on a small cluster of ordinary database machines, and since every access is by the code, the data shards cleanly by code.

How long must the code be? With 62 characters (digits, lower case, upper case), 6 characters give 62^6 = 56.8 billion codes and 7 characters give 62^7 = 3.5 trillion. Six billion URLs over five years fits in 6 characters with room to spare, but 7 leaves a thousandfold margin and makes guessing codes harder. The demo below confirms the figure: it prints 3,521,614,606,208 for the number of 7-character codes.

The cache size follows from how links are used. Link popularity is very skewed: a small share of links gets most of the clicks. If the hottest 1 percent of 100 million links, one million of them, is cached at about 120 bytes each (code plus URL plus overhead), the cache holds about 120 MB. A single Redis node can hold it, and a cache of a few gigabytes could hold far more than the working set. Expect a hit ratio above 90 percent, which cuts database reads from 20,000 a second at peak to under 2,000.

The central question is how to produce a short unique code. There are four common answers, and the right one depends on what you want to guarantee.

**Hash the URL and truncate.** Take MD5 or SHA-256 of the long URL, encode it in base62 and keep the first 7 characters. The same URL always gets the same code, which gives deduplication for free, and no coordination between servers is needed. The problem is collisions: two different URLs can share a prefix. By the birthday approximation, with N possible codes and n URLs, the expected number of colliding pairs is about n^2 / (2N). For n = 1 billion and N = 3.5 trillion, that is (10^9)^2 / (7 x 10^12), roughly 143,000 colliding pairs. So the insert must check for an existing code and, on a conflict, retry with a salt appended to the URL. That works, but every write becomes a read-then-write, and the number of retries grows as the table fills.

**A random code, checked.** Generate 7 random base62 characters, insert with a unique constraint, retry on conflict. It is simple and the codes are unguessable, but it has the same collision handling as hashing, without the deduplication benefit.

**A global counter, encoded.** Keep one counter, increment it per URL and encode the number in base62. Collisions are impossible by construction. Ids are small (the first million are at most 4 characters). The weakness is the counter itself: a single database row or ZooKeeper node taking 40 increments a second is fine, but a network call on every write is a dependency on the write path, and sequential codes let anyone enumerate every link by counting.

**A counter handed out in blocks, then scrambled.** This is the design to propose. A small allocator service hands each application server a block of, say, 1,000 consecutive ids in one call. The server hands out ids from memory with no network call and fetches a new block only when it runs out. A crashed server wastes at most the unused part of its block, up to 999 ids, which is nothing against 3.5 trillion. To stop people counting, pass each id through a reversible scramble, for example multiplication by a large odd constant modulo 2^42, which maps distinct inputs to distinct outputs and makes consecutive ids look unrelated. Then encode in base62.

The demo implements the encoder, the block allocator and the scramble. It shows that 2,500 ids need exactly 3 blocks of 1,000, that three sequential ids produce unrelated-looking codes, and that 100,000 scrambled ids are all distinct (a multiplication by an odd number modulo a power of two is a bijection, so this holds for all inputs, not only the ones tested).

The redirect status decides who owns the cache. A **301** (permanent) lets browsers and intermediaries cache the redirect forever: later clicks never reach you, which saves load but means you lose click counts, cannot change or expire the target, and cannot take a link down. A **302** (temporary) makes every click pass through your service, so analytics, expiry and abuse takedowns all work. Most shorteners use 302, or 301 with a short `Cache-Control: max-age`, and accept the load because it is small (4,000 requests a second).

A **custom alias** is a user-chosen code. It lives in the same table, and the same unique constraint protects it, so two users asking for `summer-sale` race safely: one insert wins and the other gets a conflict error. Keep the generated codes and the aliases from colliding by giving aliases a different shape (a minimum length of 8, say, or a reserved separator) and by checking reserved words such as `api` and `admin`.

**Expiry** needs two mechanisms. On read, compare `expires_at` with the current time and answer 404 or 410 when it has passed, so correctness never depends on cleanup. In the background, a sweeper deletes expired rows in small batches, using an index on the expiry time, and removes the cache entry. Put the expiry into the cache TTL too: the cache entry lives for the smaller of a default (an hour) and the time left.

**Abuse** matters more than throughput for a public shortener. Attackers use short links to hide phishing pages. Check submitted URLs against a safe-browsing list, rate-limit creation per account and per IP, allow takedown by code, and refuse to redirect to private address ranges (a server-side request forgery risk if you ever fetch the link to generate a preview).

sections.title: Failure modes and what happens to each

blocks.body:
Walk through what breaks, with numbers, because an interviewer wants to hear the system degrade gracefully.

**The cache node dies.** Every redirect becomes a database read. At the 20,000 a second peak that is a 10 times jump over the normal 2,000 misses a second. A read replica set sized for it survives; without that, the database slows and redirects time out. Mitigations: run the cache as a replicated cluster so one node loss only removes a slice, warm the replacement from the database for the hottest codes, and let the redirect service coalesce concurrent misses for the same code into one database read so a viral link does not stampede.

**The allocator is down.** Application servers keep working until their local block is used up. With 10 servers and 40 writes a second in total, each server uses about 4 ids a second, so a 1,000-id block lasts about 250 seconds, over four minutes. A longer outage means writes fail while redirects continue, which is the right priority: reads are 99 percent of the traffic. Raising the block size to 10,000 stretches the window to 40 minutes at the cost of a bigger loss per crash.

**One database shard is hot or down.** Sharding by a hash of the code spreads load evenly. If a shard is down, only the codes on it fail, unless it has a replica to promote. A single viral code is the problem a shard cannot fix, and the cache plus a CDN in front of the redirect handles it: a CDN edge can serve the redirect itself for a few seconds, which flattens a spike to a trickle at the origin.

**A region is down.** Reads are easy to serve from several regions with data replicated asynchronously, since a link created a second ago may not have arrived yet, and the right answer there is a short retry or a fallback read from the home region. Writes need one home region per code range, or an allocator per region that hands out disjoint id ranges.

**The click pipeline backs up.** Click events go to Kafka without the redirect waiting for them, so analytics lag never slows a redirect. If Kafka is unavailable, drop or buffer events locally; losing a few counts is acceptable, a slow redirect is not.
Hash-based codes dedupe but need collision handling; counters are simple but need a coordination service.
NoSQL fits the pure key-value access; relational is fine at this size with read replicas and a cache.
Read-heavy (~100:1); 7-char base62 = 3.5T codes.
Codes from a counter with range allocation (no collisions) or hash + collision check.
Redirect path: cache (Redis) → KV store; 301 cacheable vs 302 trackable.
Click analytics async via a queue, never on the redirect path.

sections.title: How do you support custom aliases?

blocks.body: Same table, insert with a uniqueness constraint on the code; reject if taken. Reserve a namespace (or length) so generated codes never collide with aliases.
301 lets browsers cache and cuts load but hides repeat clicks from analytics; 302 (or 307) keeps every click visible. Most shorteners use 302 when analytics matter.

sections.title: How do you expire links and reclaim codes?

blocks.body: Store expires_at, check it on redirect, and run a background sweeper. Don't reuse codes quickly: old links in the wild would point to new content.
Rate-limit creation per user/IP, scan destinations against malware/phishing lists, and allow takedowns.

architecture.name: WebSocket gateways
architecture.role: Hold one long-lived connection per device, authenticate once and forward messages to the chat service.
architecture.scale: 100 million concurrent connections at 100,000 to 1 million each means roughly 100 to 1,000 servers. They are stateful, unlike a normal web tier.
architecture.failure: When one dies, around 200,000 connections drop at once. Clients reconnect with backoff and jitter and sync from their last sequence number.

architecture.name: Session registry
architecture.role: A Redis hash mapping each user and device to the gateway that holds its connection, with a TTL refreshed by heartbeats.
architecture.scale: One lookup per delivery, so a replicated Redis cluster sharded by user handles hundreds of thousands of lookups a second.
architecture.failure: A stale entry sends to a gateway that no longer holds the connection. The service falls back to store, push and sync later, so a wrong route costs latency, not data.

architecture.name: Chat service and sequencer
architecture.role: Appends each message to its conversation's log with the next server-assigned sequence number, dedupes by client message id and fans out to members.
architecture.scale: About 230,000 messages a second on average and 700,000 at peak. All writes for a conversation go to one shard, so the sequence number is a simple counter there.
architecture.failure: If the shard is down, sending for those conversations cannot move elsewhere without risking disorder. Replicate with a quorum and show not sent rather than claim delivery.

architecture.name: Message store
architecture.role: A wide-column store (Cassandra or HBase) partitioned by conversation id and bucketed by month, clustered by sequence number.
architecture.scale: 20 billion messages a day at about 200 bytes is 4 TB a day and about 1.5 PB a year. Reading the latest 50 messages is a single-partition range read.
architecture.failure: A slow or lost node is hidden by replication. Very active groups are split into time buckets so no partition grows without limit.

architecture.name: Fan-out queue and push
architecture.role: Delivers a group message to each member's gateways without blocking the sender's ack, and sends push for offline devices.
architecture.scale: A group of 200 means 200 deliveries, so cap group size or fan out through a queue. Presence is sent only to users with the conversation open.
architecture.failure: Push is best effort and never relied on for correctness: the message is already stored and the app syncs when opened.

criteria.strong: Gets 230,000 messages a second average, 4 TB a day and about 100 million concurrent connections, and turns them into gateway and storage sizing.
criteria.weak: Says a lot of users and picks a database before looking at message volume.

criteria.strong: Uses a server-assigned sequence number per conversation and a client message id for idempotent retries, instead of device timestamps.
criteria.weak: Sorts by sender timestamps, so different devices show different orders, and retries create duplicates.

criteria.strong: Explains WebSocket gateways, a session registry with heartbeats, an offline path, and catch-up by last seen sequence number.
criteria.weak: Uses polling for every client or has no plan for offline devices and new devices.

criteria.strong: Partitions by conversation, stores one copy per conversation with a read pointer per member, and bounds fan-out and partition size.
criteria.weak: Stores a copy of every message per recipient and cannot compute read receipts cheaply.

criteria.strong: Covers a gateway loss, stale registry, a slow shard and reconnect floods with jitter, and keeps push as best effort only.
criteria.weak: Assumes connections never drop and does not say what happens when a whole gateway goes down.

blocks.body: Order by a per-conversation monotonically increasing id (from the partition owner or a Snowflake id with conversation affinity). The client's clientMsgId dedupes retries. Clients sort by sequence id, not arrival time.

Persist before acking the sender. Recipients ack receipt; unacked messages are re-sent on reconnect via a sync endpoint ('give me messages after seq N'). This gives at-least-once delivery with client-side dedup.
Heartbeats over the WebSocket update a presence store with TTL; publish changes only to contacts who are online, and batch them to avoid storms.

A chat system delivers messages between two users or inside groups with low latency, never loses a message, shows messages in a consistent order, and works across the user's devices, including when they are offline. Details that change the design: group size limits (a few hundred or thousands), whether history is stored forever, end-to-end encryption, and presence ("online", "typing").

Estimates: 500 million daily users send 40 messages a day, which is 20 billion messages a day, about 230,000 a second on average and 700,000 at peak. A message averages 100 bytes of text plus 100 bytes of metadata, so 20 billion x 200 bytes = 4 TB a day, about 1.5 PB a year. That volume rules out a single database, and it points at a store sharded by conversation, where all messages of one conversation sit together and are read in order.

Connections: 500 million users, perhaps 100 million online at once. A gateway server can hold about 100,000 to a million idle WebSocket connections if tuned (memory per connection of a few KB), so 100 million connections need roughly 100 to 1,000 gateway servers. Connections are long-lived and stateful, which makes the gateway tier different from a normal stateless web tier.

The client keeps one persistent connection, usually a WebSocket, to a gateway. Polling would waste bandwidth and add latency. The gateway authenticates once, then forwards messages to the chat service. The **session registry** (a Redis hash or similar) maps each user and device to the gateway that currently holds its connection, with a TTL refreshed by heartbeats. To deliver a message, the chat service looks up the recipient's gateways and sends the message to each. For a group, it loops over the members, which is why group size must be capped or messages fanned out through a queue.

**Ordering** is the subtle part. Different devices, with different clocks, must show the same order. Use a **server-assigned sequence number per conversation**: the chat service appends the message to the conversation's log and gives it the next number. Everyone sorts by that number, not by the sender's timestamp. If a conversation's writes all go to one shard, assigning the number is simple (a counter in that shard); a conversation is the natural unit of partitioning.

**Retries and duplicates.** A phone on a bad network may send a message, lose the connection before the acknowledgement, and send again. The client therefore attaches a unique client message id, and the server remembers which ids it has stored, returning the existing sequence number on a repeat. The demo shows it: two messages get sequence numbers 1 and 2, a retry of the first returns 1 and adds nothing (the log still has 3 messages after the next one), and a new message gets 3.

**Catching up.** A device that reconnects asks for everything after its last seen sequence number. The demo's device that last saw message 1 receives messages 2 and 3. This one mechanism handles offline users, new devices and gaps after a dropped connection.

Messages are append-heavy, read by conversation in order, and rarely updated. A wide-column store such as Cassandra or HBase fits: partition key is the conversation id, clustering key is the sequence number, so reading the latest 50 messages is a single-partition range read. A very active group can create a huge partition, so bucket by time (conversation id plus month) and keep the active bucket small. Old history can move to cheaper storage.

**Groups.** Sending to a group of 200 means 200 deliveries. Do the fan-out in the chat service through a queue so the sender's ack does not wait for it. Store one copy of the message per conversation, not per recipient, and track each member's read position (a sequence number) separately. That makes "read receipts" a tiny per-member counter instead of a row per message. Very large groups and channels behave more like a feed and use fan-out on read.

**Presence and typing indicators** are the most expensive features per unit of value. Each connect and disconnect, multiplied by all of a user's friends, is a flood. Reduce it: send presence only to users who currently have the conversation open, batch changes over a few seconds, treat "last seen" as approximate, and make typing indicators ephemeral messages that are never stored.

**Receipts.** Three states: sent (the server stored it), delivered (the device acknowledged), read (the user opened the conversation). Each is a small event routed back to the sender, and read state is just the member's read pointer.

**End-to-end encryption** changes the server's role: it stores and routes ciphertext it cannot read, so it cannot offer server-side search or content moderation, and multi-device support needs per-device keys (the Signal protocol design). Mention it as a requirement to clarify, then describe the design without it unless asked.

**A gateway dies.** All its connections, perhaps 200,000, drop at once. Clients reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter to avoid a stampede on the remaining gateways, and sync from their last sequence number, so nothing is lost. Capacity planning keeps spare room: if one of ten gateways fails, the other nine take 11 percent more each, which is fine, but losing a whole zone is not unless planned.

**The session registry is stale.** The chat service may send to a gateway that no longer holds the connection. The gateway reports a failure, the service falls back to the offline path (store, push, sync later), and the registry entry is cleaned up. Because messages are stored first, a wrong route costs latency, not data.

**A message store shard is slow or down.** Writes for the conversations on it fail or queue. Because the sequence number is assigned there, sending cannot continue elsewhere without risking disorder. Replicate the shard with a quorum so one node loss is invisible, and fail the send visibly (the client shows "not sent, retry") rather than claim delivery.

**Duplicate delivery.** Acks can be lost, so a recipient may receive a message twice. The client deduplicates by sequence number and ignores one it already has.

**Thundering herd at reconnect.** After a regional network problem, millions reconnect together. Rate-limit connection setup per gateway, spread reconnects with jitter, and keep the sync call cheap (a range read from the latest position).

**Push notification failures.** Push is best-effort. Never rely on it for correctness: the message is in the store, and the app syncs when opened.

**Abuse.** Rate-limit senders per user and per conversation, and apply spam checks before fan-out so one bad actor cannot send to a million users.
WebSockets (stateful, need connection-aware routing) vs long polling.
Storing messages per conversation (simple reads) vs per user inbox (simpler sync, more writes).
WebSocket gateways hold connections; a session registry maps user → gateway.
Messages persisted (Cassandra, partition by conversation) before ack; ids time-ordered.
Offline users: store and push notification; sync from last seen message id.
Group fan-out by members; big groups via per-group queues.
Per-conversation ordering from a sequence assigned by the conversation's owner shard (or Snowflake ids within one partition); clients sort by it and dedupe by message id.
Server ack = sent; recipient device ack = delivered; read event when shown. Each is a small message routed back to the sender's devices.

blocks.body: Heartbeats from connected clients update a TTL key; publish changes only to contacts who are online and subscribed, with debounce to avoid flapping.
Each device has its own connection and sync cursor; messages fan out to all of a user's devices.

architecture.name: Payment API gateway and idempotency store
architecture.role: Authenticates callers and does an atomic conditional insert of the Idempotency-Key before any work starts. A completed key returns the stored response; an in-progress key returns 409.
architecture.scale: Sized for about 580 payments per second on average and 8,000 at a promotion peak. A key lookup is a single indexed read, so it adds a few milliseconds.
architecture.failure: If the store is down the gateway must refuse new payments rather than skip the check, because skipping it allows double charges. Keys expire after a fixed window such as 24 hours.

architecture.name: Payment orchestration service
architecture.role: Saves the payment as PENDING, calls the PSP with a derived idempotency key, then writes the ledger entries, status change and outbox row in one local transaction.
architecture.scale: Stateless, scaled out behind the gateway. The PSP call is the slow step, around 1 to 3 seconds, so thread pools and timeouts are sized for it.
architecture.failure: A PSP timeout leaves the payment unknown, so it moves to PENDING_VERIFICATION and a worker queries the PSP. It never guesses success or failure.

architecture.name: Tokenized card vault
architecture.role: Stores card numbers inside the PCI-DSS boundary and hands every other service an opaque token. Only the vault and the PSP adapter ever see real card data.
architecture.scale: Lookups are by token, so reads spread evenly across shards. Keeping the vault small keeps the audit scope small.
architecture.failure: If the vault is down, new card payments fail. Keys live in an HSM and the vault is replicated across zones so one zone loss does not stop it.

architecture.name: Double-entry ledger
architecture.role: Append-only journal where every transaction has two or more postings and debits equal credits. A $100 charge posts DR $100 clearing, CR $97 merchant payable, CR $3 fee revenue.
architecture.scale: About 4 postings per payment and roughly 2 KB per payment in total. At 50 million payments a day that is about 100 GB per day, 36.5 TB per year before replication, partitioned by posting date.
architecture.failure: A primary crash mid-commit leaves no partial rows because the commit is atomic. A balance check job alerts if any transaction does not sum to zero.

architecture.name: Outbox and reconciliation service
architecture.role: The outbox streams PaymentSucceeded events to Kafka by change data capture. Reconciliation matches ledger, processor report and bank deposit every night.
architecture.scale: Outbox events are at-least-once, so consumers dedupe by event id. Reconciliation reads one settlement file set per day per processor and finishes in minutes.
architecture.failure: A mismatch goes to a suspense account and a break ticket. A daily variance above 0.005% of volume, about $5,000 on $100M, pages the treasury on-call.

criteria.strong: Stores money as integer cents in a 64-bit field with an ISO 4217 currency code, and explains why float and double drift.
criteria.weak: Uses a floating-point column or a decimal with no currency, and does not say how rounding of fees is handled.

criteria.strong: Uses a client idempotency key with an atomic insert, handles the in-progress case, and passes a derived key to the PSP so retries cannot double charge.
criteria.weak: Says retries are fine, or dedupes only in the gateway, so a PSP retry can still charge twice.

criteria.strong: Append-only double-entry postings that sum to zero, refunds as compensating entries, balances derived from postings or signed snapshots.
criteria.weak: One mutable balance column updated in place, with no audit trail and heavy row lock contention.

criteria.strong: Treats a PSP timeout as unknown, polls with the idempotency key, and uses a transactional outbox so the database and Kafka cannot disagree.
criteria.weak: Treats a timeout as failure and retries a new charge, or writes to the database and Kafka separately.

criteria.strong: Describes three-way matching, a suspense account for breaks, a variance alert threshold and seven-year retention.
criteria.weak: Stops at the successful charge and has no plan for settlement files, disputes or breaks.
