4. Iterate `right` from 0 to `s.length() - 1`:
   a. If `need[s[right]] > 0`, decrement `missing`.
   b. Decrement `need[s[right]]`.
   c. While `missing == 0` (window is valid):
      i. If `right - left + 1 < bestLen`, record `bestLen = right - left + 1` and `bestStart = left`.
      ii. Increment `need[s[left]]`.
      iii. If `need[s[left]] > 0`, increment `missing` (since an essential character was evicted).
      iv. Increment `left`.
5. Return empty string `""` if `bestLen == infinity`, otherwise `s.substr(bestStart, bestLen)`.

Complexity:
- Time: `O(|s| + |t|)` because counting `t` takes `O(|t|)` and each character in `s` enters via `right` once and leaves via `left` at most once.
- Space: `O(alphabet)` which is `O(1)` fixed auxiliary space (128 ASCII table).

Sliding window with a need-count table. Expand right; a character that t still needed reduces 'missing'. When missing is 0, the window is valid: advance left while the leftmost character is surplus (its need count is negative), recording the best window each time it is valid.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: Then drop the left character (which makes the window invalid again) and continue expanding. Every index enters and leaves the window at most once.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body:
In the reference implementation:
- `vector<int> need(128, 0);`: precomputes target counts for each character.
- `if (need[(unsigned char)s[right]]-- > 0) missing--;`: consumes character `s[right]`; decrements `missing` only when that character was needed.
- `while (missing == 0)`: enters contraction phase whenever the window is valid.
- `if (right - left + 1 < bestLen) { bestLen = right - left + 1; bestStart = left; }`: updates minimal substring bounds.
- `if (++need[(unsigned char)s[left]] > 0) missing++; left++;`: evicts `s[left]`; if it was essential, breaks the valid state to force expansion.

- `s = "ab", t = "b"`:
  - `need['b'] = 1`, `missing = 1`.
  - `right = 0 ('a')`: `need['a']` becomes -1, `missing` stays 1.
  - `right = 1 ('b')`: `need['b']` was 1 > 0, `missing` becomes 0.
  - Contract: `bestLen = 2 - 0 = 2`, `bestStart = 0`. Evict `'a'`: `need['a']` becomes 0, not > 0, so `missing` remains 0!
  - `left` becomes 1. Window `"b"`: length 1 < 2, update `bestLen = 1, bestStart = 1`. Evict `'b'`: `need['b']` becomes 1 > 0, `missing` becomes 1. `left` becomes 2.
  - Returns `s.substr(1, 1) = "b"`.
- `s = "a", t = "aa"`:
  - `missing` starts at 2. After `right = 0`, `missing` is 1. Loop finishes.
  - `bestLen` remains infinity, returns `""`.

- What if `s` is very long and contains mostly characters not in `t`?
  Filter `s` to create a list of pairs `(index, char)` containing only characters that appear in `t`, and run the two-pointer window over this filtered list.
- How does this compare to Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (LeetCode 3)?
  LeetCode 3 contracts when a duplicate is found (maintaining an invariant of at most 1 of each char), whereas LeetCode 76 expands until at least `k` of each target char are contained.

- Re-checking entire map equality inside the loop in `O(alphabet)` time rather than maintaining an integer `missing` variable.
- Forgetting that negative values in `need` represent surplus characters inside the window.
- Extracting substrings repeatedly with `s.substr()` inside the loop, adding `O(n^2)` string copying overhead.

- Sliding window technique with dual monotonic pointer schedules.
- Counting hash tables and window condition invariants.

row.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
row.complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space for the recursion (h = tree height).

extra._interviewFrontmatter:
---
id: lc-98
pattern: dfs-recursion
difficulty: medium
optimal: "O(n) time, O(h) space"
reviewed: false
---

cases.explanationMd: The 3 is in the right subtree of 5, but 3 is smaller than 5.

hints.bodyMd: Checking each node only against its direct children is not enough. What should a node really be compared against?
Every node must fall in a range set by all its ancestors, not just its parent. Think about what range a left child and a right child each inherit.
Pass a lower and an upper bound down with each node. Going left lowers the upper bound to the parent's value; going right raises the lower bound. Use 64-bit bounds for extreme values.

blocks.body: Given the root of a binary tree, decide whether it is a valid binary search tree.

In a valid one, for every node, all values in its left subtree are strictly smaller than the node's value and all values in its right subtree are strictly larger. A tree is given level by level, with null for a missing child: [1,null,2,3] is a root 1 with no left child, a right child 2, and 3 as the left child of 2.

- Are duplicate values allowed in a valid BST? No, the definition requires strictly smaller values in the left subtree and strictly larger values in the right subtree (`val <= low` or `val >= high` is invalid).
- What values can nodes hold? Values range between `-2^31` and `2^31 - 1`, covering the entire 32-bit signed integer range.
- Does verifying the local condition `node->left->val < node->val < node->right->val` suffice? No, every ancestor imposes a global boundary on all descendant subtrees.
- Can the tree be empty? Constraints indicate at least 1 node up to 10,000 nodes.

- Valid BST: `root = [2, 1, 3]`. Node 1 is strictly less than 2, and node 3 is strictly greater than 2. Valid, returns true.
- Subtree violation that passes local checks: `root = [5, 1, 4, null, null, 3, 6]`. Locally, 4 has left child 3 and right child 6, which seems ordered. However, 3 is in the right subtree of the root 5 and `3 < 5`, violating the BST property. Returns false.
- Duplicate values edge case: `root = [2, 2, 2]`. Returns false because children must be strictly smaller or larger.

A brute-force strategy performs an in-order traversal of the tree, appends all node values into an array, and checks whether the array is strictly monotonically increasing. While this runs in `O(n)` time, it uses `O(n)` auxiliary space to store all values. Alternatively, inspecting the entire subtree at every node takes `O(n^2)` time in an unbalanced tree.

Every node in a BST must fall within an open value range `(low, high)` determined by its chain of ancestors. The root starts with bounds `(-infinity, +infinity)`. When traversing into a left child, the upper bound is narrowed to `node.val` (all left descendants must be `< node.val`). When traversing into a right child, the lower bound is updated to `node.val` (all right descendants must be `> node.val`).

1. Define a helper function `ok(node, low, high)`.
2. Base case: If `node == null`, return true.
3. If `node.val <= low` or `node.val >= high`, return false.
4. Recursively validate left and right children:
   - For left child: `ok(node.left, low, node.val)`.
   - For right child: `ok(node.right, node.val, high)`.
5. In the main function, call `ok(root, LLONG_MIN, LLONG_MAX)` using 64-bit bounds so that standard 32-bit `INT_MIN` and `INT_MAX` node values are not prematurely rejected.

Complexity:
- Time: `O(n)` because each node in the tree of size `n` is visited once.
- Space: `O(h)` stack space, where `h` is the tree height (`O(log n)` for balanced trees, `O(n)` worst-case for degenerate skewed trees).

Pass down an open interval of allowed values. Start with (-infinity, +infinity). A node must lie strictly inside its interval; its left child gets (low, node.val) and its right child gets (node.val, high).
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: Use long long for the bounds: with int bounds a node holding the minimum int would be rejected by a sentinel. An in-order traversal that checks the values are strictly increasing works too.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body:
In the reference implementation:
- `bool ok(TreeNode* n, long long low, long long high)`: validates that `n` satisfies the bounding interval.
- `if (!n) return true;`: an empty subtree is unconditionally valid.
- `if (n->val <= low || n->val >= high) return false;`: rejects nodes violating ancestor bounds or containing duplicates.
- `return ok(n->left, low, n->val) && ok(n->right, n->val, high);`: tightens bounds when branching left and right.
- `isValidBST(TreeNode* root)`: passes 64-bit extremes `LLONG_MIN` and `LLONG_MAX` to avoid integer overflow issues.

- `root = [2, 1, 3]`:
  - Root 2: check against `(-inf, inf)`. Valid.
  - Left child 1: check against `(-inf, 2)`. `1 < 2`, valid.
  - Right child 3: check against `(2, inf)`. `3 > 2`, valid.
  - Result: true.
- `root = [5, 4, 6, null, null, 3, 7]`:
  - Root 5: valid with `(-inf, inf)`.
  - Right child 6: valid with `(5, inf)`.
  - Node 3 (left child of 6): check with range `(5, 6)`. But `3 <= 5`, fails immediately!
  - Result: false.

- How would you solve this iteratively without 64-bit sentinel bounds?
  Perform an iterative in-order traversal using a stack, keeping track of the previous node's value and asserting `prev < cur->val` at each step.
- Can we reconstruct a BST from only preorder traversal?
  Yes, using the upper-bound monotonicity property in `O(n)` time.

- Only checking immediate children (`node->left->val < node->val`), which misses violations deeper in subtrees.
- Using 32-bit `INT_MIN` and `INT_MAX` as default bounds, causing false failures when a node's value is actually `INT_MIN` or `INT_MAX`.
- Using `<=` or `>=` instead of `<` and `>`, accidentally permitting duplicate keys.

- Binary search tree invariants and in-order traversal properties.
- Morris in-order traversal for `O(1)` auxiliary space verification.

row.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
row.complexity: O(n) time, O(w) space where w is the widest level.

extra._interviewFrontmatter:
---
id: lc-102
pattern: bfs-level-order
difficulty: medium
optimal: "O(n) time, O(w) space"
reviewed: false
---

cases.explanationMd: An empty tree has no levels.

hints.bodyMd: You want nodes grouped by their distance from the root. Which kind of structure hands out items in the order they were added?
A queue. Start with the root, then repeatedly remove a node and add its children to the back.
Before processing a round, note how many nodes are in the queue. Process exactly that many; together they form one level.

blocks.body: Given the root of a binary tree, return its values level by level, from left to right: first the root, then its children, then their children, and so on. Return a list of lists, one per level.
A tree is given level by level, with null for a missing child: [1,null,2,3] is a root 1 with no left child, a right child 2, and 3 as the left child of 2.

- Can the root node be null? Yes, 0 nodes is possible; return an empty list `[]`.
- In what format should the result be returned? A list of lists, where each sub-list contains node values on that level ordered left to right.
- What are the tree size bounds? Between 0 and 2,000 nodes.
- Can values be negative? Yes, values range from -1,000 to 1,000.

- Multi-level tree: `root = [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]`.
  - Level 0: `[3]`.
  - Level 1: `[9, 20]`.
  - Level 2: `[15, 7]`.
  - Returned structure: `[[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]`.
- Single node tree: `root = [1]`. Level 0 is `[1]`, returns `[[1]]`.
- Empty tree: `root = []`. Returns `[]`.

A brute-force strategy computes the total height `h` of the tree, and then for every level `d` from 0 to `h - 1`, calls a recursive function that prints nodes at depth `d`. Because every level re-traverses from the root down to depth `d`, this approach takes `O(n * h)` time, which degrades to `O(n^2)` for skewed trees.

A queue processes nodes in First-In, First-Out (FIFO) order. By capturing the queue's size at the beginning of each iteration, we delineate the exact boundary of the current tree level. All nodes currently in the queue belong to this level, and any children pushed during the level's processing belong to the next level.

1. If `root == null`, return an empty list.
2. Initialize a queue with `root` and an empty list `out` to store level lists.
3. While the queue is not empty:
   a. Let `n = queue.size()`.
   b. Allocate a temporary list `level` for the current tier.
   c. Loop `n` times:
      i. Dequeue node `x`.
      ii. Append `x.val` to `level`.
      iii. If `x.left` exists, enqueue `x.left`.
      iv. If `x.right` exists, enqueue `x.right`.
   d. Append `level` to `out`.
4. Return `out`.

Complexity:
- Time: `O(n)` because every node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once.
- Space: `O(w)` auxiliary queue memory, where `w` is the maximum width of the tree (`w <= n / 2` for a complete binary tree).
Breadth-first search with a queue. At the start of each round, the queue holds exactly one level. Read its size, pop that many nodes into a list, and push their children for the next round.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: Return an empty list for an empty tree.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body:
In the reference implementation:
- `if (!root) return out;`: handles null trees immediately.
- `queue<TreeNode*> q; q.push(root);`: initiates BFS from the root.
- `int n = (int)q.size();`: snapshots the exact node count residing at the active level.
- `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)`: processes only nodes belonging to this level.
- `if (x->left) q.push(x->left); if (x->right) q.push(x->right);`: schedules next level's children into the queue.
- `out.push_back(level);`: saves the completed tier.

- `root = [1, 2, 3, null, 4, null, 5]`:
  - Level 0: queue has `[1]`. Size is 1. Pop 1, push left 2 and right 3. Level 0 is `[1]`.
  - Level 1: queue has `[2, 3]`. Size is 2. Pop 2, push right 4. Pop 3, push right 5. Level 1 is `[2, 3]`.
  - Level 2: queue has `[4, 5]`. Size is 2. Pop 4 (no children). Pop 5 (no children). Level 2 is `[4, 5]`.
  - Queue is empty, returns `[[1], [2, 3], [4, 5]]`.
- `root = []`:
  - Root is null, returns `[]`.

- How would you implement zigzag (spiral) level order traversal (LeetCode 103)?
  Alternate reversing the level array, or use a deque to push and pop from alternating ends based on level depth.
- Can this be solved using DFS?
  Yes, pass current depth as a parameter; if `depth == out.size()`, append a new list to `out`, then append `node.val` to `out[depth]`.

- Recomputing `q.size()` dynamically inside the `for` loop condition (`i < q.size()`), which causes newly pushed children to be processed on the current level.
- Failing to check if `root == null` before accessing children or pushing into the queue.
- Enqueueing null children, which requires null checks upon dequeueing.

- Breadth-first search queue mechanics on trees and graphs.
- Level-order variations including bottom-up and zigzag traversals.

row.title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 100000].
At most 100000 calls will be made to hasNext and next.
row.complexity: next and hasNext run in O(1) amortized time, using O(h) space where h is tree height.

extra._interviewFrontmatter:
---
id: lc-173
pattern: bst-properties
difficulty: medium
optimal: "O(1) amortized time, O(h) space"
reviewed: false
---

cases.explanationMd: next() repeatedly yields the next smallest in-order element: 3, 7, 9, 15, 20.

hints.bodyMd: Does the iterator need to know every value up front, or only the next value to return?
A sorted tree can be walked one step at a time while remembering only the path you are on, not all the values.
Keep a stack of nodes. Push the leftmost path when you start, then on each step pop a node and push the leftmost path of its right child.
hasNext is simply whether the stack still has something on it.

blocks.body: Implement the BSTIterator class that represents an iterator over the in-order traversal of a binary search tree (BST).

BSTIterator(root) initializes an object of the BSTIterator class. The root of the BST is given as part of the constructor. The pointer should be initialized to a non-existent number smaller than any element in the BST.
next() moves the pointer to the right, then returns the number at the pointer.
hasNext() returns true if there exists a number in the traversal to the right of the pointer, otherwise returns false.
Notice that by initializing the pointer to a non-existent smallest number, the first call to next() returns the smallest element in the BST.

Each test gives the operations in order (the class name first, then method names) and their arguments; the expected answer has one entry per operation, with null for the constructor and for methods that return nothing.

- What traversal order must the iterator yield? (In-order traversal: visiting values in strictly ascending sorted order).
- What operations must be supported? (`next()` returning the next integer, and `hasNext()` returning a boolean).
- What are the time and space constraints? (`next()` and `hasNext()` should run in $O(1)$ amortized time, using $O(h)$ auxiliary memory where $h$ is tree height, rather than $O(n)$ space).
- Is `next()` ever called when `hasNext()` is false? (Standard API assumption is that calls to `next()` are valid).
- What are the tree size bounds? ($1 \le n \le 100,000$, with at most $100,000$ calls).

- Standard BST: `root = [7, 3, 15, null, null, 9, 20]`.
  - In-order sequence is: `3, 7, 9, 15, 20`.
  - First `next()` yields 3.
  - Second `next()` yields 7.
  - `hasNext()` returns `true`.
  - Calling `next()` three more times yields 9, 15, 20.
  - Final `hasNext()` returns `false`.
- Single node tree: `root = [1]`. Initial `hasNext()` is `true`, `next()` returns 1, subsequent `hasNext()` is `false`.

A naive approach runs a full in-order traversal in the constructor, flattening the entire BST into an array or queue of size $n$. `next()` simply pops the next element from the array in $O(1)$, and `hasNext()` checks if the index is within bounds. While time complexity is $O(1)$ per operation, this requires $O(n)$ extra memory upfront. For a tree with $100,000$ nodes, allocating memory for all nodes defeats the purpose of an iterator, which should stream elements lazily using only $O(h)$ space ($O(\log n)$ on balanced trees).

Instead of flattening the entire tree upfront, we can pause the iterative in-order traversal using an explicit stack of node pointers.
In recursive in-order traversal:
1. We first walk as far left as possible, pushing nodes onto the recursion call stack.
2. The leftmost node is the smallest unvisited element.
3. When that node is popped and visited, its right subtree is explored by walking as far left as possible in the right child.
By maintaining this exact call stack explicitly, the stack contains at most $h$ nodes at any point in time. Each node in the tree is pushed onto the stack exactly once and popped exactly once across all $n$ calls to `next()`, giving amortized $O(1)$ time per operation.

1. Maintain an internal stack of node pointers `st`.
2. Define a helper method `pushLeft(node)`:
   - While `node != nullptr`:
     - Push `node` onto `st`.
     - Advance `node = node->left`.
3. Constructor `BSTIterator(root)`:
   - Call `pushLeft(root)`. The top of the stack is now the smallest element in the BST.
4. Operation `next()`:
   - Pop `curr = st.top()`.
   - Call `pushLeft(curr->right)` to load the left spine of the right subtree.
   - Return `curr->val`.
5. Operation `hasNext()`:
   - Return `!st.empty()`.

Complexity:
- Time: $O(1)$ amortized time for `next()`, strictly $O(1)$ worst-case time for `hasNext()`. Across $n$ calls to `next()`, exactly $n$ nodes are pushed and popped, totaling $2n$ stack operations.
- Space: $O(h)$ auxiliary space where $h$ is the height of the BST ($O(\log n)$ on balanced trees, $O(n)$ in the worst-case skewed tree).
Maintain an explicit stack of TreeNode pointers simulating the call stack of an in-order traversal.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: A helper function pushes a node and all of its left descendants onto the stack. The constructor calls this on root.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: next pops the top node, pushes all left descendants of its right child, and returns the popped node's value. hasNext simply checks whether the stack is non-empty.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body:
In the reference implementation:
- `stack<TreeNode*> st;`: stores the ancestor path currently being traversed.
- `void pushLeft(TreeNode* node)`: traverses down the left spine, pushing every ancestor so smaller keys precede larger keys.
- `BSTIterator(TreeNode* root)`: prepares the iterator pointing before the first element by loading the root's left descendants.
- `TreeNode* curr = st.top(); st.pop(); pushLeft(curr->right);`: consumes the in-order predecessor and advances down the successor's left branch.
- `bool hasNext() { return !st.empty(); }`: tests whether any unvisited nodes remain.

- Right-skewed tree: `1 -> 2 -> 3`.
  - Constructor pushes 1.
  - `next()` pops 1, pushes 2, returns 1.
  - `next()` pops 2, pushes 3, returns 2.
  - `next()` pops 3, stack empty, returns 3.
  - `hasNext()` returns `false`.
- Left-skewed tree: `3 -> 2 -> 1`.
  - Constructor pushes 3, 2, 1 (stack size 3).
  - First `next()` pops 1, right is null, stack has `[3, 2]`. Returns 1.
  - Subsequent calls pop 2 then 3.

- Can we implement `prev()` / bidirectional BST iterator?
  Yes, maintain two stacks or pointers, allowing backward steps by traversing right-spines instead of left-spines.
- How to achieve $O(1)$ extra memory?
  Morris Traversal modifies the tree by creating temporary predecessor thread pointers, achieving $O(1)$ space, but mutates tree pointers during traversal.
- How does this pattern apply to general binary trees (not BST)?
  The exact same stack-based in-order traversal works on any binary tree; on a BST it yields elements in sorted order.

- Flattening the tree into an array in the constructor, violating the $O(h)$ memory constraint.
- Forgetting to call `pushLeft(curr->right)` after popping a node in `next()`, missing all right-hand descendants.
- Pushing all children rather than only the left-leaning descendants.

- Iterative binary tree in-order traversal using stacks.
- Morris Traversal for $O(1)$ space in-order traversal.

row.title: Number of Islands
constraints: Each cell is the string 1 or the string 0
row.complexity: O(rows * columns) time, O(rows * columns) worst-case space for the stack.

extra._interviewFrontmatter:
---
id: lc-200
pattern: dfs-flood-fill
difficulty: medium
optimal: "O(rows * cols) time, O(rows * cols) space"
brute: same
reviewed: false
---

hints.bodyMd: When you find a land cell you have not seen before, you have found a new island. How do you avoid counting the rest of that island again?
Explore everything connected to it, moving up, down, left and right, and mark every land cell you reach as seen.
Count each new starting cell once. Marking cells as seen by changing them to water avoids needing a separate visited record.

blocks.body: You get a grid of characters, where '1' is land and '0' is water. An island is a group of land cells connected up, down, left or right (not diagonally). Count the islands.
In the tests the grid is a list of rows, each a list of the strings "1" and "0".

- Do diagonal connections count as part of the same island? No, connectivity is strictly 4-directional (up, down, left, right).
- Can the grid be empty? Constraints indicate rows and columns are between 1 and 300.
- Is modifying the grid allowed in-place? Yes, sinking visited land cells by mutating `'1'` to `'0'` saves allocating a separate visited matrix.
- What values appear in the grid? Only characters (or strings) `"1"` (land) and `"0"` (water).

- Single large island: A grid where all `'1'`s are connected into one component. After traversing the first `'1'`, all adjacent `'1'`s are marked visited, returning count 1.
- Multiple separated islands:
  - Row 0: `["1", "1", "0", "0", "0"]`
  - Row 1: `["1", "1", "0", "0", "0"]`
  - Row 2: `["0", "0", "1", "0", "0"]`
  - Row 3: `["0", "0", "0", "1", "1"]`
  - Returns 3 separate connected components.
- All water edge case: A grid filled entirely with `"0"`, returning 0.

A brute-force search is not fundamentally different in complexity, but a naive implementation might search paths without marking visited cells, causing infinite cycles between adjacent land cells. Alternatively, computing connected components via full transitive closure on an adjacency matrix takes `O((rows * cols)^2)` time, which for a 300x300 grid (`90,000` cells) would require over `8 \times 10^9` operations.
The direct approach is already optimal here.
blocks.label: brute-same

blocks.body: The grid can be modeled as an undirected graph where each `'1'` cell is a vertex and edges connect adjacent `'1'`s. The number of islands equals the number of connected components. When an unvisited `'1'` is discovered, we increment the island count and execute a flood fill (DFS or BFS) to visit and sink all reachable land cells in that component before continuing the scan.

1. Initialize `count = 0`, and get grid dimensions `rows` and `cols`.
2. Define directional vectors for 4-way movement: `(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)`.
3. Iterate `r` from 0 to `rows - 1`, and `c` from 0 to `cols - 1`:
   a. If `grid[r][c] == "1"`:
      i. Increment `count`.
      ii. Start an iterative DFS (or BFS) from `(r, c)`.
      iii. Mark `grid[r][c] = "0"` and push `(r, c)` onto a stack.
      iv. While the stack is not empty, pop `(x, y)` and inspect its 4 neighbors. For each neighbor `(nx, ny)` within bounds that equals `"1"`, set `grid[nx][ny] = "0"` and push onto the stack.
4. Return `count`.

Complexity:
- Time: `O(rows * cols)` because every cell is visited by the outer loops once and touched by the flood fill at most once.
- Space: `O(rows * cols)` worst-case auxiliary space for the DFS stack if the entire grid is land.

Scan every cell. When you meet a '1', add one to the count and flood-fill the island from there, setting each land cell you touch to '0' so it is never counted again. The flood fill visits the four neighbours of each cell.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: An explicit stack or queue instead of recursion avoids deep recursion on a 300 by 300 grid of land.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body:
In the reference implementation:
- `const int dr[4] = {1, -1, 0, 0}, dc[4] = {0, 0, 1, -1};`: encapsulates 4-directional orthogonal neighbor offsets.
- `if (grid[r][c] != "1") continue;`: skips already sunken land or water cells.
- `count++;`: registers discovery of an independent landmass.
- `grid[nx][ny] = "0";`: immediately sinks a neighboring land cell upon enqueueing to prevent duplicate stack entries.
- `vector<pair<int, int>> st;`: utilizes an explicit stack to avoid deep call-stack recursion on large grids.

- `grid = [["1", "0"], ["0", "1"]]`:
  - `(0, 0)` is `"1"`: `count` becomes 1. Sink `(0, 0)`. Neighbors `(1, 0)` and `(0, 1)` are `"0"`. Flood fill terminates.
  - `(0, 1)` is `"0"`, `(1, 0)` is `"0"`.
  - `(1, 1)` is `"1"`: `count` becomes 2. Sink `(1, 1)`.
  - Return 2.
- `grid = [["0"]]`: returns 0 immediately.

- What if the grid cannot be modified?
  Maintain an auxiliary 2D boolean `visited` array of size `rows x cols` or use a hash set of coordinate pairs.
- Can this be solved using Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find)?
  Yes, initialize a DSU with all land cells as independent sets, union adjacent land cells, and return the number of distinct roots.

- Marking a cell as visited when popping from the stack rather than when pushing, leading to redundant pushes and memory exhaustion on large grids.
- Using unbounded recursive DFS, which can trigger stack overflow when `rows * cols = 90,000`.
- Allowing diagonal transitions when the problem specifies orthogonal adjacency.

- Flood fill algorithm and connected-component labeling.
- Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) for dynamic graph connectivity.

row.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
constraints: The tree is a valid binary search tree
row.complexity: O(h + k) time, O(h) space.

extra._interviewFrontmatter:
---
id: lc-230
pattern: bst-properties
difficulty: medium
optimal: "O(h + k) time, O(h) space"
reviewed: false
---

hints.bodyMd: In a binary search tree, which order of visiting nodes lists the values from smallest to largest?
In-order: left subtree, then the node, then right subtree. The k-th node visited is the answer.
Walk in-order with an explicit stack and count the visited nodes. Stop as soon as the count reaches k, so you never visit more than needed.

blocks.body: Given the root of a binary search tree and a number k, return the k-th smallest value among all the nodes, counting from 1.
A tree is given level by level, with null for a missing child: [1,null,2,3] is a root 1 with no left child, a right child 2, and 3 as the left child of 2.

- Is `k` 1-indexed? Yes, `k` counts from 1 up to the total number of nodes `n`.
- Is the tree guaranteed to be a valid BST? Yes, all left subtree keys are smaller, and right subtree keys are larger.
- Can `k` be greater than the number of nodes in the tree? Constraints guarantee `1 <= k <= n <= 10,000`.
- Can the tree be modified during this query? Modifying the tree is not required, and in-place reads preserve concurrent access.

- Simple BST: `root = [3, 1, 4, null, 2]`, `k = 1`.
  - In-order traversal visits nodes in ascending order: 1, 2, 3, 4.
  - The 1st smallest element is 1.
- Larger tree: `root = [5, 3, 6, 2, 4, null, null, 1]`, `k = 3`.
  - Sorted order: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
  - The 3rd smallest element is 3.

A brute-force strategy traverses the entire BST (using any traversal order like preorder or BFS), appends all `n` values to an array, sorts the array, and returns the element at index `k - 1`. Sorting takes `O(n log n)` time and `O(n)` extra memory. Even an in-order traversal that writes all `n` elements into an array takes `O(n)` time and `O(n)` space, which does unnecessary work when `k` is small.

An in-order traversal (left, root, right) of a binary search tree visits nodes in strictly ascending numerical order. Instead of traversing the whole tree, we can simulate an iterative in-order traversal using an explicit stack, stopping immediately once we have popped exactly `k` nodes.

1. Initialize an empty stack of node pointers and set pointer `cur = root`.
2. While `cur != null` or the stack is not empty:
   a. Push `cur` onto the stack and move `cur = cur.left` until `cur` is null (reaching the minimum of the current subtree).
   b. Pop node `cur` from the stack.
   c. Decrement `k`. If `k == 0`, return `cur.val` immediately.
   d. Set `cur = cur.right` to explore the right subtree.
3. If loop exits without returning, return -1 (unreachable given constraints).

Complexity:
- Time: `O(h + k)` where `h` is the height of the tree. Reaching the smallest node takes `O(h)`, and visiting the first `k` elements takes `O(k)` steps. In balanced trees, this is `O(log n + k)`.
- Space: `O(h)` stack space to store nodes along the current path (`O(log n)` on average, `O(n)` worst-case).

In-order traversal visits a BST in increasing order. Use an explicit stack: push the left spine, pop a node (that is the next smallest), then continue with its right subtree. Decrement k each time you pop; when it hits 0, return that node's value.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: This stops after k pops, so it costs O(h + k) instead of walking the whole tree.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body:
In the reference implementation:
- `vector<TreeNode*> st; TreeNode* cur = root;`: tracks the path of left-leaning ancestors.
- `while (cur) { st.push_back(cur); cur = cur->left; }`: descends to the smallest unprocessed element.
- `cur = st.back(); st.pop_back();`: retrieves the next smallest node in sorted order.
- `if (--k == 0) return cur->val;`: decrements the rank counter and immediately terminates when the target rank is hit.
- `cur = cur->right;`: pivots to the right subtree to continue the in-order sequence.

- `root = [3, 1, 4, null, 2], k = 1`:
  - Push 3, push 1. `cur` reaches null.
  - Pop 1. `--k` becomes 0. Return `1`.
- `root = [3, 1, 4, null, 2], k = 2`:
  - Push 3, push 1.
  - Pop 1. `--k` becomes 1. `cur` moves to `1->right` (2).
  - Push 2.
  - Pop 2. `--k` becomes 0. Return `2`.

- What if the BST is modified frequently (insertions/deletions) and you need to find the kth smallest element often?
  Augment each tree node with a `subtree_size` count. At any node, if `left.size + 1 == k`, return `node.val`; if `k <= left.size`, go left; otherwise `k -= left.size + 1` and go right. This achieves `O(h)` query time.
- Can we achieve `O(1)` space?
  Yes, using Morris in-order traversal, though it temporarily modifies tree pointers during traversal.

- Traversing the entire tree into an array when `k` might be 1, doing `O(n)` work instead of `O(h)`.
- Off-by-one errors with `k` (e.g. checking `k == 0` before decrementing).
- Using preorder or postorder traversal instead of inorder, which does not visit nodes in sorted order.

- Morris in-order tree traversal algorithm.
- Order statistic trees and augmented data structures.

row.title: Design Twitter
row.complexity: postTweet, follow, unfollow O(1); getNewsFeed O(f log f) where f is about 10 times the number of followees.

extra._interviewFrontmatter:
---
id: lc-355
pattern: design-problems
difficulty: medium
optimal: "O(1) post/follow, O(F log F) getNewsFeed time, O(U + T) space"
reviewed: false
---

cases.explanationMd: After user 1 follows user 2, tweet 6 shows up above tweet 5 because it is newer. After unfollow, only user 1's own tweet is left.

hints.bodyMd: A feed only shows ten tweets. Does a tweet that is not among its author's ten most recent ever matter?
A tweet outside its author's newest ten can never reach the feed's top ten, so only the newest ten per person are candidates.
Give each tweet a global increasing time, gather the newest ten from the user and from each person they follow, then merge them and keep the top ten.
Store follows in a set so that repeated follow or unfollow calls do nothing when the link already exists or is missing.

blocks.body: Design a small Twitter: users post tweets, follow and unfollow each other, and read a news feed.

postTweet(userId, tweetId) makes the user post a tweet with this id (ids are unique). getNewsFeed(userId) returns the ids of the 10 most recent tweets in the user's feed, newest first; the feed holds the user's own tweets and the tweets of everyone the user follows. If there are fewer than 10, return all of them. follow(followerId, followeeId) makes the follower follow the followee (nothing changes if they already do). unfollow(followerId, followeeId) stops it (nothing changes if they did not). A user always sees their own tweets.

Each test gives the operations in order (the class name first, then method names) and their arguments; the expected answer has one entry per operation, with null for the constructor and for methods that return nothing.

- What operations must be supported? (`postTweet(userId, tweetId)`, `getNewsFeed(userId)`, `follow(followerId, followeeId)`, and `unfollow(followerId, followeeId)`).
- What appears in a user's news feed? (The 10 most recent tweet IDs posted by the user themselves or by anyone they follow, ordered newest first).
- Does a user always see their own tweets in their feed? (Yes, a user always sees their own tweets even without following themselves).
- Can a user follow themselves? (Constraints state `followerId != followeeId`).
- What if there are fewer than 10 tweets available? (Return all available tweets, sorted newest first).

- Follow, post, and unfollow flow:
  - User 1 posts tweet 5: `postTweet(1, 5)`. Feed for user 1: `[5]`.
  - User 1 follows user 2: `follow(1, 2)`.
  - User 2 posts tweet 6: `postTweet(2, 6)`.
  - Feed for user 1: `[6, 5]` (tweet 6 is newer than tweet 5).
  - User 1 unfollows user 2: `unfollow(1, 2)`.
  - Feed for user 1: `[5]` (user 2's tweets are immediately removed).

A naive fan-out-on-write approach maintains a precomputed feed list for each user. When `postTweet` is called, find all followers of `userId` and prepend `tweetId` to their feed lists. However, when `follow` or `unfollow` occurs, reconstructing the follower's entire feed history takes $O(T)$ time where $T$ is the total tweet count. Alternatively, pulling every tweet ever posted across all followed users and sorting all of them takes $O(T_{\text{total}} \log T_{\text{total}})$, which degrades as tweet counts grow.

Notice that a news feed only requires at most **10** most recent tweets in total.
Therefore, for any individual user or followee, **only their last 10 tweets can ever possibly appear in the final top-10 result**. Older tweets beyond their personal top-10 cannot make the cut.
- Use a global logical timestamp counter (`clock++`) to timestamp each tweet.
- When `getNewsFeed(userId)` is called, collect at most the last 10 tweets from `userId` and from each user in `follows[userId]`.
- If a user follows $F$ people, we gather at most $10 \times (F + 1)$ candidate tweets. Sorting these candidates (or merging them with a max-heap) takes $O(F \log F)$ time, independent of total historical tweet volume.

1. Maintain internal state:
   - `int clock = 0`: global monotonic timestamp generator.
   - `unordered_map<int, vector<pair<int, int>>> tweets`: maps `userId` to a list of `{time, tweetId}`.
   - `unordered_map<int, unordered_set<int>> follows`: maps `followerId` to the set of `followeeId`s.
2. Operation `postTweet(userId, tweetId)`:
   - Append `{clock++, tweetId}` to `tweets[userId]`.
3. Operation `follow(followerId, followeeId)`:
   - Insert `followeeId` into `follows[followerId]`.
4. Operation `unfollow(followerId, followeeId)`:
   - Erase `followeeId` from `follows[followerId]`.
5. Operation `getNewsFeed(userId)`:
   - Initialize `vector<pair<int, int>> pool`.
   - Helper `addLast10(u)`: if `u` has tweets, append the last $\min(10, \text{size})$ elements from `tweets[u]` into `pool`.
   - Call `addLast10(userId)` (user always sees their own tweets).
   - For each followee `f` in `follows[userId]`: call `addLast10(f)`.
   - Sort `pool` in descending order of timestamp.
   - Extract up to the first 10 `tweetId`s from `pool` and return them.

Complexity:
- Time: `postTweet`, `follow`, and `unfollow` run in $O(1)$ average time. `getNewsFeed` takes $O(F \log F)$ time where $F$ is the number of followees ($F \le 500$, so pool size $\le 5000$).
- Space: $O(U + T)$ auxiliary space where $U$ is the number of users and $T$ is the total number of tweets and follow relationships stored.
Give every tweet a time from a counter that goes up by one on each post. Store each user's tweets as a list of (time, id) and each user's followees as a set.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: To build a feed, take at most the last 10 tweets of the user and of each followee (older ones can never be among the 10 newest overall), sort them by time from newest to oldest and return the ids of the first 10. A heap that merges the users' lists does the same with less sorting.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body:
In the reference implementation:
- `tweets[userId].push_back({clock++, tweetId});`: assigns an incremental logical timestamp to preserve global post ordering.
- `follows[followerId].insert(followeeId);`: set-based relationship mapping handles duplicate follow calls idempotently.
- `for (int i = max(0, (int)v.size() - 10); i < (int)v.size(); i++) pool.push_back(v[i]);`: bounds candidate pooling to at most 10 per author.
- `sort(pool.rbegin(), pool.rend());`: orders candidate tweets from most recent to oldest.
- `feed.push_back(pool[i].second);`: extracts the top 10 tweet IDs.

- User with >10 tweets: User 1 posts 12 tweets. `getNewsFeed(1)` returns tweets 12 down to 3 (exactly 10 tweets).
- User with 0 tweets: Returns empty list `[]`.
- Unfollowing non-followed user: Idempotent no-op via `follows[followerId].erase(followeeId)`.
- Concurrent followees: Multiple followees post interspersed tweets; timestamps ensure chronological ordering across authors.

- Can we optimize `getNewsFeed` using a k-way merge instead of sorting?
  Yes, each user's tweet list is already sorted by time. Using a max-heap of size $F + 1$, we can perform a k-way merge extracting the 10 largest elements in $O(F + 10 \log F)$ time.
- How does real Twitter architecture handle this?
  Celebrities with millions of followers use pull-on-read (fan-out on read) with caching, while standard users use push-on-write (fan-out on write) to precompute follower timelines.
- How to handle pagination?
  Accept an optional `cursor_time` or `max_tweet_id` parameter to fetch the next 10 tweets older than the cursor.

- Inserting all tweets of followed users into `pool` rather than only the last 10, leading to $O(T_{\text{total}} \log T_{\text{total}})$ performance degradation.
- Forgetting that a user must see their own tweets even if they follow no one.
- Not ensuring timestamps are strictly distinct across tweets (using wall-clock time with identical millisecond resolution instead of an atomic counter).

- K-way merge algorithm using priority queues.
- Fan-out on read vs Fan-out on write timeline architecture patterns.

row.title: Design Hit Counter
constraints: All the calls are being made to the system in chronological order (i.e., timestamp is monotonically increasing).
At most 300000 calls will be made to hit and getHits.
row.complexity: hit is O(1) amortized, getHits is O(1) amortized, space is O(k) where k is the number of hits within the 300-second window.

extra._interviewFrontmatter:
---
id: lc-362
pattern: design-problems
difficulty: medium
optimal: "O(1) amortized time per operation, O(W) space"
reviewed: false
---

cases.explanationMd: At t=4, hits within [0, 4] are 1, 2, 3 (count 3). At t=300, hits within [0, 300] are 1, 2, 3, 300 (count 4). At t=301, hit at 1 has expired (> 300 seconds old), remaining are 2, 3, 300 (count 3).

hints.bodyMd: Hits arrive in time order and old hits stop counting. Where does the oldest hit sit?
The oldest hit is always the first to leave the window, and new hits always join at the newest end.
Use a first-in first-out queue. Add each hit at the back, and on each query remove hits from the front that are too old.
A hit exactly 300 seconds before the query has expired, so the window keeps only hits newer than that.

blocks.body: Design a hit counter which counts the number of hits received in the past 5 minutes (i.e., the past 300 seconds).

Your system should accept a timestamp parameter (in seconds granularity), and you may assume that calls are being made to the system in chronological order (i.e., timestamp is monotonically increasing). Several hits may arrive roughly at the same time.
Implement the HitCounter class:
HitCounter() initializes the object of the hit counter system.
hit(timestamp) records a hit that happened at timestamp (in seconds). Several hits may happen at the same timestamp.
getHits(timestamp) returns the number of hits in the past 5 minutes from timestamp (i.e., past 300 seconds, timestamp - 300 < t <= timestamp).

Each test gives the operations in order (the class name first, then method names) and their arguments; the expected answer has one entry per operation, with null for the constructor and for methods that return nothing.

- What time window does the hit counter measure? (The past 5 minutes, which corresponds to the past 300 seconds: $timestamp - 300 < t \le timestamp$).
- Do calls arrive in chronological order? (Yes, the problem guarantees that calls to `hit` and `getHits` have monotonically non-decreasing timestamps).
- Can multiple hits occur at the exact same timestamp? (Yes, multiple hits may occur at the same second).
- What is the granularity of timestamps? (Seconds granularity; timestamps are positive integers up to $2 \cdot 10^9$).
- What are the call limits? (Up to 300,000 calls to `hit` and `getHits`).

- Window expiration walkthrough:
  - `hit(1)`, `hit(2)`, `hit(3)`
  - `getHits(4)` $\implies$ all 3 hits fall within $(4 - 300, 4]$, returns 3.
  - `hit(300)` $\implies$ total 4 hits recorded.
  - `getHits(300)` $\implies$ window is $(0, 300]$; hits at 1, 2, 3, 300 all count, returns 4.
  - `getHits(301)` $\implies$ window is $(1, 301]$; hit at 1 has expired ($1 \le 301 - 300$), so only 2, 3, 300 remain; returns 3.

A naive approach appends every hit timestamp into an unbounded dynamic array. On each `getHits(timestamp)`, it iterates from the beginning of the array, counting how many elements satisfy $t > timestamp - 300$. With up to 300,000 calls, scanning the full list on every `getHits` takes $O(N)$ per query, resulting in $O(N^2) \approx 9 \times 10^{10}$ operations and severe Time Limit Exceeded.

Because timestamps arrive in monotonically increasing order:
1. Incoming hits always enter at the newest edge of time.
2. Expired hits always leave from the oldest edge of time.
This matches a **First-In, First-Out (FIFO) queue**.
Whenever `getHits(timestamp)` is called, any timestamp at the front of the queue that is $\le timestamp - 300$ has permanently expired and will never be valid for any future query. By popping expired elements from the front of the queue, the remaining queue size is precisely the count of active hits in the past 300 seconds.

1. Maintain a FIFO queue `queue<int> q` storing hit timestamps.
2. Operation `hit(timestamp)`:
   - Push `timestamp` into `q`.
3. Operation `getHits(timestamp)`:
   - While `q` is not empty and `q.front() <= timestamp - 300`:
     - Pop the expired element: `q.pop()`.
   - Return `q.size()`.

Complexity:
- Time: `hit` runs in $O(1)$ time. `getHits` runs in $O(1)$ amortized time, because each hit timestamp is pushed to the queue once and popped at most once across the entire lifetime of the system.
- Space: $O(W)$ auxiliary space where $W$ is the number of hits received within any rolling 300-second window (at most 300,000 elements).
Because timestamps arrive in non-decreasing order, keep a queue of hit timestamps.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: hit pushes timestamp onto the queue.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: getHits evicts all elements from the front of the queue whose timestamp is less than or equal to timestamp - 300, and returns the remaining queue size.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body:
In the reference implementation:
- `queue<int> q;`: stores chronological stream of hit events.
- `q.push(timestamp);`: records each arrival in $O(1)$.
- `while (!q.empty() && q.front() <= timestamp - 300) q.pop();`: evicts expired events from the head of the sliding window.
- `return q.size();`: reports the current valid hit count in $O(1)$.

- Burst at same second: `hit(10)` called 3 times. `getHits(10)` returns 3. `getHits(309)` returns 3. `getHits(310)` pops all three, returns 0.
- No hits recorded: `getHits(1)` and `getHits(300)` on a fresh counter return 0.
- Large gaps between queries: `hit(100)`, `hit(200)`, then `getHits(900)`. All items are popped in the loop, returning 0 without errors.

- What if millions of hits arrive in the same second (scaling for high write throughput)?
  A raw queue would grow to millions of elements. Instead, use a **circular array of 300 buckets**, each storing `pair<int, int>` for `(timestamp, hit_count)`. Indexing by `timestamp % 300` caps space to strictly $O(1)$ (300 buckets) and aggregates simultaneous hits in $O(1)$ time.
- How to make the circular bucket approach thread-safe?
  Use atomic integers or bucket-level locks / striped mutexes across the 300 buckets so concurrent threads can increment counts without contention.
- How to support distributed hit counting across multiple servers?
  Each server maintains local circular buffers; a central aggregator or Redis sliding-window counter merges bucket sums periodically.

- Using `<` instead of `<=` in `q.front() <= timestamp - 300`: hits occurring at exactly $timestamp - 300$ are outside the open interval $(timestamp - 300, timestamp]$ and must be popped.
- Not handling multiple hits at the same timestamp.
- Attempting to binary search an unbounded list without trimming old entries, leading to unbounded memory growth.

- Sliding window counter algorithms.
- Circular buffer design for high-throughput rate limiters and metric counters.

row.title: Linked List Random Node
constraints: The number of nodes in the linked list will be in the range [1, 10000].
At most 10000 calls will be made to getRandom.
row.complexity: O(n) time per call with O(1) extra space, or O(1) time with O(n) space.

extra._interviewFrontmatter:
---
id: lc-382
pattern: combinatorics-probability
difficulty: medium
optimal: "O(n) time, O(1) space"
reviewed: false
---

hints.bodyMd: You cannot know the list length without walking it. Can you still pick a node while seeing each node only once?
If you have seen i nodes so far, the new node should take over the choice with a chance of one in i.
Reservoir sampling: keep one answer, and for the i-th node replace it with probability one over i. Every node then has an equal chance at the end.
Start with the first node as the answer, so a single-node list always returns its value.

blocks.body: Given a singly linked list, return a random node's value from the linked list. Each node must have the same probability of being chosen.
Implement the Solution class:
Solution(head) initializes the object with the head of the singly-linked list head.
getRandom() chooses a node randomly from the list and returns its value. All the nodes of the list should be equally likely to be chosen.

The judge tests getRandom on single-element lists so that the chosen node's value is uniquely determined. Write your solution to handle arbitrary length lists using reservoir sampling (O(1) memory) or storage.

Each test gives the operations in order (the class name first, then method names) and their arguments; the expected answer has one entry per operation, with null for the constructor and for methods that return nothing.

- Is the linked list length known in advance? (No, singly linked lists do not provide length in $O(1)$ without an initial traversal).
- What should be the probability distribution? (Every node must have an identical, uniform probability $1/N$ of being chosen).
- What are the memory constraints? (The interviewer typically evaluates Reservoir Sampling to achieve true $O(1)$ extra space, without copying all elements into an array).
- Can the list be empty? (Constraints guarantee at least 1 node; $1 \le N \le 10,000$).
- Can node values be negative? (Yes, $-10,000 \le Node.val \le 10,000$).

- Single node: `head = [1]`. `getRandom()` returns 1 with $100\%$ probability.
- Two nodes: `head = [1, 2]`.
  - Start with `ans = 1`.
  - Node 2 is visited ($i = 2$): probability of picking node 2 is $1/2$.
  - Both 1 and 2 are returned with probability $0.5$.
- Three nodes: `head = [1, 2, 3]`.
  - Node 3 ($i = 3$): replaces reservoir with probability $1/3$.
  - Node 1 or 2 survived step 2 with probability $1/2$, and survives step 3 with probability $2/3 \implies \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{3}$. Every element has probability $1/3$.

A naive approach traverses the linked list during the constructor and copies all $N$ values into an `std::vector<int>`. Then `getRandom()` calls `rand() % values.size()` in $O(1)$ time. While fast for repeated queries, this consumes $O(N)$ extra space. If the linked list is massive (e.g. Billions of elements streaming across a network), storing the entire list in memory is impossible.

We use **Reservoir Sampling** (Alan G. Waterman's Algorithm R), which samples from a stream of unknown or unbounded length in $O(1)$ extra space.
- Set the initial candidate answer to the head value: `ans = head->val`.
- For the $i$-th node visited ($i = 2, 3, \dots, N$), generate a random integer in $[0, i - 1]$. If the random value is 0 (which occurs with probability $1/i$), replace `ans` with `curr->val`.
- Mathematical induction:
  - The $k$-th element is selected at step $k$ with probability $1/k$.
  - For each subsequent step $j > k$, it is NOT replaced with probability $1 - 1/j = \frac{j-1}{j}$.
  - The overall probability that element $k$ is the final choice after $N$ elements is:
    $\frac{1}{k} \times \frac{k}{k+1} \times \frac{k+1}{k+2} \times \dots \times \frac{N-1}{N} = \frac{1}{N}$.

1. Constructor `Solution(head)`:
   - Store the pointer to the `head` of the linked list.
2. Operation `getRandom()`:
   - Initialize `ans = head->val`.
   - Set pointer `curr = head->next` and counter `i = 2`.
   - While `curr != nullptr`:
     - If `rand() % i == 0`:
       - Overwrite `ans = curr->val`.
     - Advance `curr = curr->next`.
     - Increment `i++`.
   - Return `ans`.

Complexity:
- Time: $O(1)$ initialization; $O(n)$ time per `getRandom()` call, where $n$ is the number of nodes in the linked list.
- Space: $O(1)$ auxiliary space since only a few pointer and integer counter variables are used.
Use Reservoir Sampling to select a random node with uniform probability while using O(1) extra memory.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: Initialize the result with the head node's value. Traverse subsequent nodes: for the i-th node visited (1-based), replace the chosen value with node->val with probability 1/i (using rand() % i == 0).
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: By induction, after n nodes, each node has probability (1/k) * (k/(k+1)) * ... * ((n-1)/n) = 1/n of being the final result.
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body:
In the reference implementation:
- `int ans = head->val;`: initializes the reservoir with the first element (guaranteed $100\%$ if $n = 1$).
- `int i = 2;`: tracks the 1-based index of the candidate element currently being evaluated.
- `if (rand() % i == 0) ans = curr->val;`: simulates a Bernoulli trial with success probability $1/i$.
- `curr = curr->next; i++;`: advances through the single linked list stream sequentially.

- Single node: `[42]`. Loop condition `curr = head->next` is null. Loop does not execute; returns 42.
- Large list: `[1, 2, ..., 10000]`. Traverses through all nodes, dynamically updating the reservoir without requiring multiple passes or knowing length upfront.
- Negative numbers: `[-10]`. Values pass through untouched, returning $-10$.

- What if $k$ random nodes need to be chosen instead of 1?
  Maintain an array reservoir of size $k$. Fill the reservoir with the first $k$ elements. For element $i > k$, pick a random integer $r \in [0, i - 1]$; if $r < k$, replace `reservoir[r]` with the new element.
- What if `getRandom` is called much more frequently than list updates, and memory is available?
  Cache all elements into a vector in $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space; `getRandom` then runs in strictly $O(1)$ time per call.
- What if nodes arrive across a distributed cluster?
  Assign each item a random priority $u \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)$, and take the item with the maximum priority.

- Using `rand() % (i + 1)` instead of `rand() % i`, distorting the replacement probability away from $1/i$.
- Assuming the list length can be measured without a traversal.
- Trying to choose a random index $r \in [0, n - 1]$ by first walking the list to count $n$, which requires two passes over the list instead of a single stream pass.

- Reservoir Sampling (Algorithm R).
- Streaming algorithms and uniform sampling without replacement.

row.title: Random Pick with Weight
constraints: pickIndex will be called at most 10000 times.
row.complexity: Constructor O(n) time and O(n) space; pickIndex runs in O(log n) time.

extra._interviewFrontmatter:
---
id: lc-528
pattern: combinatorics-probability
difficulty: medium
optimal: "O(n) init, O(log n) pickIndex time, O(n) space"
reviewed: false
---

hints.bodyMd: If you picked uniformly from the list, what would each index's chance be? How could the weights change that?
Lay the weights end to end on a line. Each index owns a piece as long as its weight, so a uniformly random point on the line picks indices by weight.
Build running totals, pick a random number from one to the total, and binary search the totals for the first one that reaches it.
Use inclusive ranges so both the number 1 and the total are valid picks, and check the indices at the edges.

blocks.body: You are given a 0-indexed array of positive integers w where w[i] describes the weight of the ith index.
You need to implement the function pickIndex(), which randomly picks an index in the range [0, w.length - 1] (inclusive) and returns it. The probability of picking an index i is w[i] / sum(w).
For example, if w = [1, 3], the probability of picking index 0 is 1 / (1 + 3) = 0.25 (i.e., 25%), and the probability of picking index 1 is 3 / (1 + 3) = 0.75 (i.e., 75%).
The judge tests pickIndex on single-weight arrays so that the answer is uniquely determined (index 0). Write your solution to handle arbitrary weights using prefix sums and binary search.

Each test gives the operations in order (the class name first, then method names) and their arguments; the expected answer has one entry per operation, with null for the constructor and for methods that return nothing.

- How is the probability of picking index $i$ calculated? (The probability of picking index $i$ is exactly $w[i] / \sum w$).
- Are weights guaranteed to be strictly positive? (Yes, $1 \le w[i] \le 100,000$).
- Can the total weight exceed a 32-bit signed integer? (With $10,000$ weights up to $100,000$, max total sum is $10^4 \times 10^5 = 10^9$, which fits comfortably in a standard signed 32-bit integer).
- What is the return value of `pickIndex()`? (An integer index $i \in [0, w.length - 1]$ chosen according to the weight distribution).
- What are the query bounds? ($w.length \le 10,000$, with at most $10,000$ calls to `pickIndex()`).

- Two weights: `w = [1, 3]`.
  - Total weight is $1 + 3 = 4$.
  - Index 0 has weight 1 ($25\%$ probability).
  - Index 1 has weight 3 ($75\%$ probability).
  - Prefix sums are `[1, 4]`. Generating random integer in $[1, 4]$: 1 maps to index 0; 2, 3, 4 map to index 1.
- Equal weights: `w = [2, 2, 2]`. Total weight 6. Each index gets range of length 2, resulting in an exact uniform $1/3$ probability each.

A naive approach expands the weight array by duplicating each index $i$ exactly $w[i]$ times into a large array of size $S = \sum w$ (e.g. `[0, 1, 1, 1]`). Then `pickIndex()` simply chooses a random uniform index from $[0, S - 1]$ in $O(1)$. However, if weights sum to $10^9$, allocating an array of size $10^9$ requires 4 GB+ of memory, causing Memory Limit Exceeded during initialization.
Another naive approach generates a random number and linearly scans through weights in $O(n)$ time per pick, which is too slow for 10,000 calls.

Think of the weights as contiguous disjoint segments laid end-to-end on a 1D number line from $1$ to $totalSum = \sum w$.
- Index 0 occupies range $[1, w[0]]$.
- Index 1 occupies range $[w[0] + 1, w[0] + w[1]]$.
- Index $i$ occupies range $[\text{prefix}[i-1] + 1, \text{prefix}[i]]$.
The length of index $i$'s segment is exactly $w[i]$, so a uniformly chosen random integer in $[1, totalSum]$ falls into index $i$'s interval with probability $w[i] / totalSum$.
Because the prefix sums are strictly increasing, we can locate the interval containing the random number using **binary search** (`std::lower_bound` / `bisect_left`) in $O(\log n)$ time.

1. Constructor `Solution(w)`:
   - Create a prefix sum array `prefix`.
   - Iterate through `w`, accumulating the running sum and appending it to `prefix`.
   - The total sum is `prefix.back()`.
2. Operation `pickIndex()`:
   - Generate a random integer `val` uniformly in the range $[1, \text{totalSum}]$: `val = (rand() % totalSum) + 1`.
   - Perform binary search (`lower_bound`) on `prefix` to find the smallest index where `prefix[idx] >= val`.
   - Return `idx`.

Complexity:
- Time: Constructor takes $O(n)$ time to build prefix sums. Each call to `pickIndex()` takes $O(\log n)$ time for the binary search.
- Space: $O(n)$ auxiliary space to store the prefix sums of length $n$.
Compute running prefix sums of the weight array w during construction. The total sum is prefix.back().
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: To pick an index, generate a random target integer uniformly in the range [1, total].
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body: Use binary search (std::lower_bound) to locate the smallest index whose prefix sum is greater than or equal to the target. This index corresponds to the interval containing target, yielding the exact probability w[i] / sum(w).
blocks.label: idea

blocks.body:
In the reference implementation:
- `prefix.push_back(sum);`: accumulates cumulative upper boundaries for each index's weight window.
- `int total = prefix.back();`: retrieves the total combined weight.
- `int val = (rand() % total) + 1;`: samples a 1-indexed random point uniformly across $[1, total]$.
- `return lower_bound(prefix.begin(), prefix.end(), val) - prefix.begin();`: finds the first prefix sum $\ge val$ in $O(\log n)$.

- Single element: `w = [10]`. `prefix = [10]`, `total = 10`. Random values in $[1, 10]$ all have `lower_bound` at index 0. Returns 0 with $100\%$ probability.
- Two distinct weights: `w = [1, 3]`. `prefix = [1, 4]`.
  - If random value is 1: `lower_bound` returns index 0 ($25\%$).
  - If random value is 2, 3, or 4: `lower_bound` returns index 1 ($75\%$).
- Large weights: `w = [100000]`. Prefix sum safely stays within integer range, returns 0.

- How to achieve $O(1)$ pick time?
  Use **Walker's Alias Method** (Vose's algorithm), which precomputes an alias table in $O(n)$ time and samples any discrete distribution in strictly $O(1)$ time.
- What if weights are updated dynamically?
  Use a Binary Indexed Tree (Fenwick Tree) or Segment Tree: updating a weight takes $O(\log n)$, and binary lifting on the Fenwick tree allows sampling in $O(\log n)$.
- What if `rand()` has insufficient resolution for large sums?
  Standard `rand()` in C++ has `RAND_MAX = 32767` on some platforms; use `std::mt19937` with `std::uniform_int_distribution<int>(1, total)` for proper 32-bit random precision.

- Generating random values in $[0, total - 1]$ instead of $[1, total]$ when using `lower_bound`: offset mismatch can shift probabilities into the wrong index buckets.
- Using 0-indexed prefix sums where `prefix[0] = 0`, leading to off-by-one errors in the returned index.
- Memory explosion by expanding weights into an explicit element array.

- Inverse Transform Sampling over cumulative distribution functions (CDF).
- Walker's Alias Method for $O(1)$ discrete random sampling.

body.why: n! operations is about 479 million at n = 12, so trying every order is allowed. The authors want you to enumerate, with some pruning.
body.falseFriend: A tiny n can also be a trap for bitmask DP (n up to 20); read the number carefully.

body.why: 2^20 is about a million, so every subset can be a state. A mask of used items is the state, or you simply enumerate subsets.
body.falseFriend: Under n = 12 plain backtracking over permutations is enough; bitmask DP helps from about 15.

body.why: 2^40 is far too big but 2^20 twice is easy: enumerate each half and join the results with sorting or hashing.

body: O(log n) insert, find, erase, lower_bound

body.fits: Try every order: permutations, full backtracking, brute force with little pruning.
Every subset: bitmask DP, include/exclude recursion, subset enumeration.
Meet in the middle: split in two halves, enumerate each, join with sort or hash.

cses-permutations.title: Permutations

cses-bit-strings.title: Bit Strings

cses-trailing-zeros.title: Trailing Zeros
cses-trailing-zeros.why: Legendre formula: count factors of 5 in n!.

cses-coin-piles.title: Coin Piles
cses-coin-piles.why: Solve 2a + b = x and a + 2b = y via integer division and bounds.

cses-palindrome-reorder.title: Palindrome Reorder
cses-palindrome-reorder.why: Character frequency parity: at most one odd count, mirror the pairs.

cses-creating-strings.title: Creating Strings
cses-creating-strings.why: Recursion with backtracking or next_permutation to enumerate unique anagrams.

cses-grid-coloring-i.title: Grid Coloring I

cses-mex-grid-construction.why: Constructive mex assignment across rows and columns using diagonal offsets.

cses-ferris-wheel.title: Ferris Wheel
cses-ferris-wheel.why: Greedy two-pointer pairing of heaviest and lightest child under weight limit.

cses-concert-tickets.why: Binary search on multiset using upper_bound to find largest ticket <= budget.

cses-restaurant-customers.title: Restaurant Customers

cses-sum-of-two-values.title: Sum of Two Values

cses-building-roads.why: Connected components using BFS/DFS or Disjoint Set Union (DSU).

cses-round-trip.why: Cycle detection in undirected graph using DFS back-edge detection.

cses-monsters.why: Multi-source BFS: propagate monster arrival times, then check escape path.

cses-shortest-routes-i.title: Shortest Routes I
cses-shortest-routes-i.why: Single-source shortest paths on non-negative weighted graph via Dijkstra's algorithm.

cses-cycle-finding.title: Cycle Finding
cses-cycle-finding.why: Negative cycle detection and extraction using Bellman-Ford / SPFA.

cses-course-schedule.why: Topological sort on directed graph using Kahn's algorithm (in-degrees) or DFS.

cses-longest-flight-route.title: Longest Flight Route
cses-longest-flight-route.why: Longest path in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) using topological order DP.

cses-game-routes.title: Game Routes
cses-game-routes.why: Count paths from 1 to n in a DAG using topological order DP.

cses-flight-discount.title: Flight Discount
cses-flight-discount.why: State-space Dijkstra on 2 layers (coupon unused vs coupon used).

cses-static-range-sum-queries.why: Prefix sum array to answer static range sum queries in O(1) time.

cses-static-range-minimum-queries.why: Sparse table with binary powers for O(1) static range minimum queries.

cses-dynamic-range-sum-queries.why: Binary Indexed Tree (Fenwick tree) or Segment Tree for point update, range sum.

cses-subordinates.why: Tree DFS subtree size aggregation from leaves to root.

cses-tree-diameter.title: Tree Diameter
cses-tree-diameter.why: Two BFS passes or tree DP to compute max distance between two tree nodes.

cses-exponentiation.title: Exponentiation
cses-exponentiation.why: Binary exponentiation computing a^b mod 10^9+7 in O(log b) time.

cses-counting-divisors.title: Counting Divisors
cses-counting-divisors.why: Sieve of Eratosthenes or prime factorization to compute divisor counts.

cses-common-divisors.title: Common Divisors
cses-common-divisors.why: Bucket frequency count and GCD sieve from max value down to 1.

cses-binomial-coefficients.title: Binomial Coefficients
cses-binomial-coefficients.why: Precomputed factorials and modular inverse via Fermat's Little Theorem for nCr.

cses-fibonacci-numbers.title: Fibonacci Numbers
cses-fibonacci-numbers.why: 2x2 matrix exponentiation to compute nth Fibonacci number in O(log n).

cses-string-matching.title: String Matching
cses-string-matching.why: KMP algorithm (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) or Z-algorithm for linear pattern matching.

cses-dynamic-range-minimum-queries.title: Dynamic Range Minimum Queries
cses-dynamic-range-minimum-queries.why: Iterative segment tree with point assignment and range minimum in O(log n).

cses-range-xor-queries.title: Range Xor Queries
cses-range-xor-queries.why: Prefix xor works like prefix sums because x ^ x = 0, so a range is two prefixes xored.

cses-range-update-queries.title: Range Update Queries
cses-range-update-queries.why: A Fenwick tree over the difference array turns range add and point read into two point updates and one prefix sum.

cses-forest-queries.title: Forest Queries
cses-forest-queries.why: Two-dimensional prefix sums answer any rectangle count in O(1) by inclusion and exclusion.

cses-forest-queries-ii.title: Forest Queries II
cses-forest-queries-ii.why: A two-dimensional Fenwick tree supports toggling one square and counting a rectangle, both in O(log^2 n).

cses-hotel-queries.title: Hotel Queries
cses-hotel-queries.why: A max segment tree lets you find the leftmost position with enough capacity by walking down the tree.

cses-list-removals.why: Removing the k-th remaining element is an order-statistic query: a Fenwick tree finds it by binary descent.

cses-salary-queries.why: Compress every salary that ever appears, then a Fenwick tree over values counts how many lie in a range.

cses-prefix-sum-queries.title: Prefix Sum Queries
cses-prefix-sum-queries.why: Each segment tree node stores its sum and its best prefix; merging two nodes is a one-line formula.

cses-subarray-sum-queries.title: Subarray Sum Queries
cses-subarray-sum-queries.why: Maximum subarray sum under updates: each node keeps sum, best prefix, best suffix and best inside.

cses-pizzeria-queries.title: Pizzeria Queries
cses-pizzeria-queries.why: Split the distance |i - k| into two cases and keep two minimum trees over p[i] - i and p[i] + i.

cses-missing-coin-sum-queries.why: The classic smallest-unreachable-sum greedy, made fast per range by summing only values below a threshold in a persistent tree.

cses-movie-festival-queries.why: The greedy 'earliest finishing movie next' becomes a jump pointer per movie, and binary lifting counts jumps inside a time window.

cses-tree-matching.why: Maximum matching on a tree: greedily pair each unmatched node with its unmatched parent, leaves first.

cses-tree-distances-i.title: Tree Distances I
cses-tree-distances-i.why: Farthest node from every node: it is always one end of a diameter, so two BFS runs from the ends are enough.

cses-tree-distances-ii.title: Tree Distances II
cses-tree-distances-ii.why: Rerooting: the sum of distances to every node, computed from the parent's sum in O(1) per node.

cses-company-queries-i.title: Company Queries I
cses-company-queries-i.why: k-th ancestor queries with binary lifting: jump by powers of two in O(log n) per query.

cses-company-queries-ii.title: Company Queries II
cses-company-queries-ii.why: Lowest common ancestor of two employees by binary lifting: equalise depths, then jump both up together.

cses-distance-queries.title: Distance Queries

cses-subtree-queries.title: Subtree Queries

cses-path-queries.title: Path Queries
cses-path-queries.why: Root-to-node sums under point updates: an update becomes a range add over the node's subtree in Euler order.

cses-path-queries-ii.title: Path Queries II
cses-path-queries-ii.why: Maximum on a tree path with point updates: heavy-light decomposition cuts any path into O(log n) array ranges.

cses-distinct-colors.title: Distinct Colors
cses-distinct-colors.why: Number of distinct values per subtree: Euler tour plus offline distinct-count queries with a Fenwick tree.

cses-finding-a-centroid.title: Finding a Centroid
cses-finding-a-centroid.why: A centroid keeps every remaining component at most n / 2: walk the subtree sizes to find it.

cses-fixed-length-paths-i.title: Fixed-Length Paths I
cses-fixed-length-paths-i.why: Counting paths of an exact length: centroid decomposition counts the paths through each centroid in linear time.

cses-fixed-length-paths-ii.title: Fixed-Length Paths II
cses-fixed-length-paths-ii.why: Counting paths with length in a range: centroid decomposition with a Fenwick tree over depths.

cses-josephus-queries.title: Josephus Queries
cses-josephus-queries.why: Recursive reduction of Josephus elimination order.

cses-exponentiation-ii.title: Exponentiation II
cses-exponentiation-ii.why: Euler's totient theorem to reduce tower of exponents modulo 10^9 + 7.

cses-sum-of-divisors.title: Sum of Divisors
cses-sum-of-divisors.why: Floor division summation over sqrt(n) blocks.

cses-prime-multiples.title: Prime Multiples
cses-prime-multiples.why: Inclusion-exclusion principle over prime multiples with overflow check.

cses-counting-coprime-pairs.title: Counting Coprime Pairs
cses-counting-coprime-pairs.why: Mobius inversion counting coprime pairs in O(maxA log maxA).

cses-creating-strings-ii.title: Creating Strings II
cses-creating-strings-ii.why: Multinomial coefficient with precomputed modular inverse factorials.

cses-distributing-apples.title: Distributing Apples
cses-distributing-apples.why: Stars and bars formula using modular combinations.

cses-christmas-party.title: Christmas Party
cses-christmas-party.why: Derangements counting using dynamic programming recurrence.

cses-bracket-sequences-i.title: Bracket Sequences I
cses-bracket-sequences-i.why: Catalan number computed via modular binomial coefficients.

cses-counting-necklaces.title: Counting Necklaces
cses-counting-necklaces.why: Burnside's lemma summing over gcd rotations modulo 10^9 + 7.

cses-nim-game-i.title: Nim Game I
cses-nim-game-i.why: Bouton's theorem: xor-sum of heap sizes determines the first player win.

cses-point-location-test.title: Point Location Test
cses-point-location-test.why: 2D cross product determining left, right, or touch orientation.

cses-line-segment-intersection.title: Line Segment Intersection
cses-line-segment-intersection.why: 2D line segment intersection with orientation tests and bounding boxes.

cses-polygon-area.title: Polygon Area
cses-polygon-area.why: Shoelace formula computing exact 2 * Area of a polygon.

cses-point-in-polygon.title: Point in Polygon
cses-point-in-polygon.why: Ray-casting algorithm with boundary collinearity detection.

cses-polygon-lattice-points.title: Polygon Lattice Points
cses-polygon-lattice-points.why: Pick's theorem combining Shoelace area and perimeter gcd points.

cses-minimum-euclidean-distance.title: Minimum Euclidean Distance
cses-minimum-euclidean-distance.why: Sweep-line with active y-interval std::set in O(n log n).

cses-convex-hull.title: Convex Hull
cses-convex-hull.why: Andrew's monotone chain algorithm preserving collinear boundary points.

cses-finding-borders.title: Finding Borders
cses-finding-borders.why: KMP prefix function chain in ascending order.

cses-finding-periods.title: Finding Periods
cses-finding-periods.why: Z-algorithm finding all valid string period lengths.

cses-minimal-rotation.title: Minimal Rotation
cses-minimal-rotation.why: Booth's linear-time lexicographical minimal string rotation.

cses-required-substring.title: Required Substring
cses-required-substring.why: KMP DFA automaton combined with dynamic programming.

cses-palindrome-queries.why: Dual Fenwick tree polynomial rolling hash supporting point updates and palindrome queries.
