body.waste: It looks up the same partner or count again and again with a nested loop.
body.fix: Remember what you have seen in a hash map and ask the map once per item.

body.waste: It recomputes the sum of the same range for many queries or many starting points.
body.fix: Store running totals once; any range sum becomes a subtraction.

body.waste: It applies the same update to many ranges one cell at a time.
body.fix: Write the change at the two ends of the range in a difference array and sum once at the end.

body.question: MVCC vs two-phase locking?
points: 2PL: growing phase acquires locks, shrinking releases; strict 2PL holds until commit.
Shared locks for reads, exclusive for writes; row vs page vs table granularity.
MVCC: writers create new versions; readers see a snapshot without locking.
Optimistic (version check at commit) for low contention; pessimistic (lock first) for high contention.

body.question: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking for an inventory decrement during a flash sale?
points: 2PL: growing phase acquires locks, shrinking releases; strict 2PL holds until commit.
Shared locks for reads, exclusive for writes; row vs page vs table granularity.
MVCC: writers create new versions; readers see a snapshot without locking.
Optimistic (version check at commit) for low contention; pessimistic (lock first) for high contention.

body.question: Why are B+ trees used instead of binary search trees on disk?
points: B+ tree: high fan-out, shallow (3-4 levels for billions of rows), leaves linked for range scans.
Clustered index = table stored in key order (InnoDB primary key); secondary indexes point to it.
Composite (a, b): useful for a or a+b, not b alone; equality columns before range columns.
Index unused when: function on the column, leading wildcard LIKE, implicit casts, low selectivity.

body.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
body.why: The single best book for system design interviews. Chapters 5-9 cover replication, partitioning, transactions and consistency.

body.title: The System Design Primer
body.why: Free overview of building blocks with worked designs. Good for a first pass and for revision.

body.title: Site Reliability Engineering (free online)
body.why: How Google runs production: SLOs, monitoring, incident response, release engineering.

body.title: Service Level Objectives (SRE book chapter)
body.why: Defines SLI / SLO / SLA properly and how to pick them. Short and very interview-relevant.

body.title: High Performance Browser Networking (free online)
body.why: TCP, TLS, HTTP/2 and latency explained with numbers. The networking chapters are the best short treatment.

body.title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (free online)
body.why: Clear, free OS textbook. Read the virtualization and concurrency parts for interview depth.

body.title: CMU 15-445 Database Systems (lectures and notes)
body.why: How databases work inside: B+ trees, query execution, concurrency control and recovery.

body.title: Use The Index, Luke (free online)
body.why: SQL indexing for developers: composite index order, why an index isn't used, pagination.

body.title: PostgreSQL: Transaction Isolation
body.why: Exactly which anomalies each isolation level allows in a real database.

body.title: Design Patterns catalog
body.why: Every classic pattern with intent, structure and code. Use it to check you can explain when to use each.

body.title: SOLID
body.why: The five principles with links to each original source.

body.title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store
body.why: Consistent hashing, quorums, vector clocks, hinted handoff. Read this before designing any key-value store.

body.title: The Google File System
body.why: Single master, chunk servers, replication. The ancestor of HDFS and many blob stores.

body.title: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters
body.why: The batch processing model: map, shuffle, reduce, and how it handles failures.

body.title: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data
body.why: Wide-column model, tablets, SSTables and memtables (LSM). Explains HBase and Cassandra's storage layer.

body.title: The Chubby lock service for loosely-coupled distributed systems
body.why: Coarse-grained locks and leader election as a service. Read with the ZooKeeper paper.

body.title: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database
body.why: External consistency with TrueTime, Paxos groups and 2PC across them.

body.title: Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure
body.why: Where distributed tracing (spans, trace ids, sampling) comes from.

body.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft)
body.why: Leader election and log replication explained clearly. Section 5 is the core.

body.title: Raft visualization and resources
body.why: Interactive visualization: watch elections and log replication happen.

body.title: ZooKeeper: Wait-free coordination for Internet-scale systems
body.why: Znodes, watches, ephemeral nodes, and how locks and leader election are built on them.

body.title: Cassandra: A Decentralized Structured Storage System
body.why: Dynamo-style distribution plus Bigtable-style storage. Short and practical.

body.title: Scaling Memcache at Facebook
body.why: Look-aside caching at huge scale: leases against thundering herds, regional invalidation.

body.title: The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data
body.why: Why an append-only log is the core abstraction behind Kafka, replication and stream processing.

body.title: Apache Kafka documentation: Design
body.why: Partitions, consumer groups, replication and delivery semantics, from the source.

body.title: The world beyond batch: Streaming 101
body.why: Event time vs processing time, windows and watermarks. The vocabulary of stream processing.

body.title: CAP Twelve Years Later: How the "Rules" Have Changed
body.why: Brewer's own clarification: CAP is about behaviour during partitions, not a three-way pick.

body.title: Please stop calling databases CP or AP
body.why: Why labelling databases CP/AP misleads, and what to say instead.

body.title: Read the limits and turn n into a time budget
body.body: Before the story, find the largest input size. A computer does about 10^8 simple steps in a second, so the size tells you the kind of algorithm the problem expects. n = 20 invites subsets, n = 5,000 invites two nested loops, n = 10^5 invites sorting and heaps, n = 10^9 invites a formula or binary search.
ask: What is the biggest n (and the second biggest dimension, like k or the number of queries)?
Which complexity fits that n in about 10^8 steps?
Is the value range huge (10^9, 10^18) or tiny (letters, digits)? That changes hash maps and counting arrays.

body.title: Name the shape of the input
body.body: Say it in one word: array, string, linked list, tree, graph, grid, intervals, a stream of numbers, or a design with operations. The shape alone removes half of the patterns. Also note whether it is sorted and whether it can change over time.
ask: Is the data sorted, sortable, or in a fixed order I must keep?
Is it fixed, or do updates and queries arrive over time?
Is a graph hiding here (a grid, dependencies, states, words one letter apart)?

body.title: Say exactly what is asked for
body.body: Is the output one best value, a count of ways, every solution, a yes or no, a position, an order, or a changed structure? The difference between 'the minimum' and 'all the ways' is the difference between DP or greedy and backtracking. A count of ways with a large answer usually says 'modulo 10^9 + 7'.
ask: Do I return a value, a count, a list of all answers, a boolean, or an object?
Do they want the best, the first found, or all of them?
What must hold (contiguous, a subsequence, distinct, non-overlapping)?

hash-map.label: Hash map / counting
hash-map.when: You need to know whether you have seen something, how often, or which group it belongs to, and a nested loop would be too slow.
hash-map.key: Trade memory for time: walk the data once, and ask the map for the partner, the count or the group before (or while) you store the current item.
watch: Look up the partner before inserting yourself, or an element can pair with itself (equal values in Two Sum).
Pick a canonical key for groups: a sorted word or a 26-count tuple for anagrams, a tuple for coordinates.
Values small and bounded (letters, 1..n)? A count array is faster and simpler than a map.
If the map keys are the answer you want in sorted order, a plain hash map will not give it to you.

template.code:
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}                      # value -> index where we saw it
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        if target - x in seen:     # ask for the partner first
            return [seen[target - x], i]
        seen[x] = i
    return []

variations.label: Complement lookup
variations.when: Two items must add up to, or differ by, a target; pairs with a property.
variations.key: Compute what the partner would have to be and look it up while scanning.

variations.label: Group by a canonical key
variations.when: Group anagrams, strings with the same shape, points on one line.
variations.key: Turn every item into a key that is equal for all members of a group, then bucket by it.

variations.label: Count frequencies
variations.when: Top k frequent, majority, is it an anagram, can letters build a word.
variations.key: One pass to count, then read the counts (sort them, heap them, or bucket by count).

variations.label: Set of values, start at the beginning
variations.when: Longest run of consecutive numbers in unsorted data.
variations.key: Put all values in a set; only start counting at x when x - 1 is missing, so each run is walked once.

variations.label: Remember the first position
variations.when: Longest span between two equal states (equal prefix, equal balance).
variations.key: Store the earliest index of each state; a later equal state gives the longest span.

prefix-sums.label: Prefix sums / difference array
prefix-sums.when: Many range-sum questions on a fixed array, a subarray sum equal to a target with negatives allowed, or many range updates applied before one read.
prefix-sums.key: pre[j] - pre[i] is the sum of the items between i and j, so any range sum is one subtraction. Run the idea in reverse (a difference array) to make a range update cost two writes.
watch: Seed the counter map with {0: 1}, or a prefix that equals the target on its own is missed.
The prefix array has n + 1 entries; most off-by-one bugs are here.
Sums can pass 32 bits when n and values are large; use 64-bit in C++ and Java.
With negative numbers a sliding window fails; prefix sums plus a map still work.

template.code:
from collections import defaultdict

def count_subarrays_with_sum(nums, k):
    seen = defaultdict(int)
    seen[0] = 1                    # the empty prefix
    pre = ans = 0
    for x in nums:
        pre += x
        ans += seen[pre - k]       # earlier prefixes that leave exactly k
        seen[pre] += 1
    return ans

variations.label: Static range sum
variations.when: Many queries sum(i..j) on data that does not change.
variations.key: Build pre once; each query is pre[j + 1] - pre[i].

variations.label: Subarray sum equals k
variations.when: Count or find subarrays with a given sum, negatives allowed.
variations.key: Count earlier prefixes equal to current - k with a hash map.

variations.label: Difference array
variations.when: Many 'add v to every item from l to r' updates, one read at the end.
variations.key: Add v at l and subtract v at r + 1, then take a running sum.

variations.label: 2D prefix sums
variations.when: Many rectangle sums in a matrix.
variations.key: P[r][c] = cell + up + left - up-left; a rectangle is four lookups.

variations.label: Prefix sums with modulo
variations.key: Two prefixes with the same remainder mod k bound a subarray whose sum is divisible by k.

two-pointers.label: Two pointers
two-pointers.when: Sorted data (or data you may sort) and a pair or triple with a target; or an in-place edit of an array or string.
two-pointers.key: Two indices walk toward each other or in the same direction, and every step throws away options that cannot be the answer, so the scan is linear.
watch: Sorting loses the original indices; keep them if the answer needs indices.
Skip equal neighbours when you must not report duplicates (3Sum).
Opposite ends: be able to say why moving that pointer cannot lose the answer.
Same direction: the slow pointer marks the finished part, the fast pointer reads ahead.

template.complexity: O(n) time after sorting, O(1) space

variations.label: Opposite ends
variations.when: Pair sum in sorted data, container with most water, palindrome check.
variations.key: Start at both ends and move the side that can only make the answer better.

variations.label: Read and write pointer
variations.when: Remove duplicates, move zeroes, filter in place.
variations.key: The fast pointer reads every item; the slow pointer writes only the items you keep.

variations.label: 3Sum and 4Sum
variations.when: Triples or quadruples that add to a target.
variations.key: Sort, fix one (or two) items, and two-pointer the rest; skip equal values.

variations.label: Walk two sorted inputs
variations.when: Merge, intersect or compare two sorted arrays.
variations.key: One pointer per input; advance the one with the smaller item.

variations.label: Partition by a rule
variations.when: Sort colours, put evens first, split around a pivot.
variations.key: Keep regions for 'done low', 'unknown' and 'done high' and move the boundaries.

body.when: The answer is a subarray or substring that satisfies a rule: longest without repeats, smallest with a sum, count with sum k, best total.

body.label: Sorted or sortable data, a target, a position, or an order
body.when: Pairs or triples with a target, a position in sorted data, a minimum feasible value, or the order of items matters.

body.title: Longest stretch without a repeated letter
body.statement: Given a string, find the length of its longest substring in which no character appears twice.
steps: Read the limit: the string can have 5 * 10^4 characters, so n^2 pairs of ends is too slow; aim for O(n).
The word is 'substring', so the answer is a contiguous part: two indices describe it.
The rule (no repeats) can be restored by moving the left end forward, so a window fits.
Keep the last seen position or a count per letter; when the new letter repeats, move the left end past its earlier copy.
After each step the window is valid; record its length.
body.brute: Check every pair of ends and test for repeats: O(n^2) pairs times O(n) to check. Even with a set per start it is O(n^2), which is too slow at n = 5 * 10^4.
body.trap: Moving the left end backwards. When a repeat appears at an old index, jump the left end to max(left, old + 1), never to a smaller value.

body.title: Count the stretches that add up to k
body.statement: Given integers (which can be negative) and a target k, count the contiguous parts whose sum is exactly k.
steps: The word 'contiguous' suggests a window, but read the numbers: they may be negative.
Negative numbers mean growing the window can decrease the sum, so shrinking logic fails. Drop the window.
A subarray sum is a difference of two prefix sums: sum(i..j) = pre[j + 1] - pre[i].
So at each position ask: how many earlier prefixes equal current prefix - k? Store prefix counts in a map.
Seed the map with {0: 1} so parts that start at the beginning count.
body.brute: For every start, extend the end and keep a running sum: O(n^2). With n up to 2 * 10^4 this passes the sample but not a stricter limit, and it rescans the same parts.
body.trap: Forgetting the empty prefix {0: 1}, which makes every subarray starting at index 0 uncounted, and using a sliding window despite negative numbers.

body.title: The slowest eating speed that still finishes in time
body.statement: Piles of bananas, h hours. Each hour you pick one pile and eat up to speed k bananas from it. Find the smallest k that finishes every pile within h hours.
steps: The question asks for the smallest speed such that something is possible: a threshold.
If speed k works then any faster speed works too, so the answer lies on a one-way boundary.
Checking one speed is easy: hours needed = sum of ceil(pile / k). That is O(n).
Binary search k between 1 and the largest pile; each step runs the check.
Total cost O(n log max pile), which fits n = 10^4.
body.brute: Try k = 1, 2, 3, ... until the check passes: up to max pile times n work, which is too slow when piles are up to 10^9.
body.trap: Using integer division instead of a ceiling in the check, and setting the upper bound too low (it must be at least the largest pile).
